## {#hero background-color="#0d1730" data-menu-title="Title slide"}

::: {.three-bg data-three="hero" data-prevent-swipe=""}
:::

::: {.hero-text}
[An interactive introduction]{.eyebrow}

[Classical and Bayesian<br>Causal Inference]{.hero-title}

[Did the treatment work — or were the people who got it *different to begin with*? This deck shows how to tell the two apart, step by step, with simulations you can play with.]{.lead}

[<span>Potential outcomes</span><span>Causal graphs</span><span>Estimation</span><span>Natural experiments</span><span>Bayesian inference</span>]{.topics}

[Jhonier Rangel · Ravi Kalia, PhD · November 14, 2026]{.byline}

[<kbd>→</kbd> begin · <kbd>F</kbd> fullscreen · <kbd>M</kbd> menu · <kbd>S</kbd> speaker view with notes · [Versión en español](index.html){.langlink lang="es"}]{.hint}
:::

::: {.notes}
Welcome. The whole deck answers one question: when we see that people who got a treatment did better, how do we know the treatment caused it, rather than the treated people being different to begin with? The background animation is the idea in miniature: a web of associations (blue) with one causal path from a treatment T to an outcome Y (orange). Our job is to isolate that path. No prior causal inference is assumed — only probability, regression, and Bayes' rule.
:::

## Why should you care? {data-menu-title="Motivation"}

**Every method in this deck answers one deceptively simple question: did the intervention actually change anything?**

- A hospital adopts a new treatment, and its patients look healthier. Were they already less sick when they were chosen?
- A tutoring program raises test scores. Were the students who signed up already improving?
- A city installs speed cameras after a terrible year, and crashes fall. Was it the cameras, or would the next year have been better anyway?

::: {.block .alert data-title="The thread for the whole deck"}
Association tells you what happened **together**. Causal inference compares what happened with what **would have happened** had we acted differently. Graphs, estimators, and priors are all tools for making that comparison honest.
:::

::: {.notes}
Open with the three stories and ask the room to vote: in each case, is the improvement caused by the intervention? Most people will hesitate, and that hesitation is the point. In every story there is a plausible alternative explanation: the groups were different to begin with (hospital, tutoring), or things would have changed anyway (cameras: an unusually bad year tends to be followed by a more normal one, which is called regression to the mean). The rest of the deck is about turning that hesitation into a precise, answerable question.
:::

## What you need, what you'll learn {data-menu-title="Goals"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.block data-title="You should be comfortable with"}
- Probability, conditional probability, expectation
- Conditional expectation and the law of iterated expectations
- Linear and logistic regression
- Confidence intervals and the CLT
- Bayes' rule; a little R or Python
:::

[No prior causal inference is assumed. Every new term is defined when it first appears.]{.small .muted}
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.block .intuition data-title="By the end you will be able to"}
1. **Pose the question precisely**: name the treatment, the outcome, the population, and the *estimand* (the exact quantity you want).
2. **Draw the story**: build a causal graph and use it to decide what to adjust for, and what *not* to.
3. **Choose an estimator**: know when regression, weighting, or Bayesian methods fit (each is explained when we get there).
4. **Interrogate the answer**: check that the groups are comparable, test sensitivity to things nobody measured, and report uncertainty honestly.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Set expectations. The mathematics in this deck is no harder than what students already know from probability and regression; what is new is the way of thinking. The hard part of causal inference is not computing an estimate, it is deciding which comparison actually answers the question. Point out the four goals map onto the pipeline on the next slide. Words like estimand, causal graph, and weighting are deliberately left undefined here; each gets a definition and an example when it first appears.
:::

## The anatomy of a causal analysis {data-menu-title="Anatomy of an analysis"}

```{=html}
<div class="pipeline"><div><b>1 · Question</b>What effect, for whom?</div><div><b>2 · Estimand</b>The precise target: ATE, ATT…</div><div><b>3 · Identification</b>Assumptions that link it to data</div><div><b>4 · Estimation</b>Regression, IPW, AIPW, Bayes</div><div><b>5 · Uncertainty</b>CIs, posteriors, sensitivity</div></div>
```

| Stage | Example: two kidney-stone surgeries, A and B | Where in this deck |
|:----------|:-------------------------------------|:----------------------|
| 1 · Question | Does surgery A succeed more often than surgery B? For which patients? | Foundations |
| 2 · Estimand | Success rate if *everyone* got A, minus if *everyone* got B | Potential outcomes |
| 3 · Identification | Doctors chose who got A, so make sure we compare *similar* patients | Potential outcomes, Causal graphs |
| 4 · Estimation | Turn that comparison into a number from the patient records | Classical estimation, Bayesian |
| 5 · Uncertainty | How precise is it? What if we missed something? | Estimation, Designs & sensitivity, Bayesian |

[Terms in the strip (ATE, ATT, IPW, AIPW…) are each defined when they first appear. Every section title shows this strip with its stages highlighted; when you feel lost, come back here.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
This is the map of the whole course. The key idea is that stages 2 and 3 come before any statistics. Stage 3, identification, is the uniquely causal step: it asks whether, under stated assumptions, the quantity we want can be written in terms of things we can observe. Only then does estimation (stage 4) begin, and that part looks like ordinary statistics. The kidney-stone column previews the running example, which is introduced properly two slides from now. A common student mistake is to jump straight to stage 4: run a regression, read off a coefficient, and call it an effect.
:::

## Our running example: kidney stones {data-menu-title="Running example"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
A real study of **700 patients** with kidney stones (Charig et al., 1986):

- **Treatment A**: open surgery (a large incision).
- **Treatment B**: percutaneous nephrolithotomy, a *keyhole* procedure through a small incision.
- **Outcome**: did the treatment succeed?
- **Doctors** decided who got which treatment. Nobody flipped a coin.
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
| Treatment | Successes | Success rate |
|:----------|:---------:|:------------:|
| A (open) | 273 / 350 | **78.0 %** |
| B (keyhole) | 289 / 350 | **82.6 %** |

[Which treatment would you choose for your next patient?]{.big}

The study also recorded each patient's **stone size**: small or large. The next slide explains why that matters.
:::
::::

::: {.block .example data-title="Hold your answer"}
B looks better by 4.6 percentage points. Before this first section ends you will see why that conclusion is wrong, and by the end of the deck you will be able to say how much better the *right* treatment is, and how sure we can be.
:::

::: {.notes}
This example comes back in every section, so take a moment with it. Ask for a show of hands: who would choose B? Most will. Do not reveal anything yet. Stress the last bullet: doctors chose the treatment, so the two groups of patients may differ in ways that matter. Everything we do later (potential outcomes, graphs, propensity scores, Bayesian models) will be applied to these same 700 patients, so students can see each method give an answer to the same question. Stone size, mentioned under the table, is the one variable besides treatment and outcome that the study recorded; the next slide explains what it means and why it matters.
:::

## Small stones, large stones {data-menu-title="Stone size"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
A **kidney stone** is a hard lump of minerals that forms in the kidney. Before treatment, each stone was measured and put in one of two groups:

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 420 200" width="100%" height="210" style="font-family:'Source Sans 3',sans-serif;font-size:17px" role="img" aria-label="A small stone fits inside a 2 cm circle; a large stone spills out of it">
  <g fill="#d9c7a7" stroke="#14213d" stroke-width="2">
    <path d="M71 76 C71 61 83 55 94 57 C107 57 113 67 112 77 C113 89 101 96 90 95 C78 95 71 87 71 76 Z"/>
    <path d="M238 74 C237 40 268 28 294 37 C320 18 364 34 365 66 C376 92 352 122 320 114 C298 128 259 122 250 103 C235 96 236 86 238 74 Z"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="none" stroke="#c8742b" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4">
    <circle cx="92" cy="76" r="42"/><circle cx="302" cy="76" r="42"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="#14213d" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="92" y="150" font-weight="700">Small: under 2 cm</text><text x="92" y="172" fill="#5b6478">357 patients</text>
    <text x="302" y="150" font-weight="700">Large: 2 cm or more</text><text x="302" y="172" fill="#5b6478">343 patients</text>
  </g>
  <text x="210" y="196" text-anchor="middle" fill="#c8742b" font-size="15">dashed circle = 2 cm across, same scale for both</text>
</svg>
```
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.block data-title="Size changes the outcome"}
A large stone is harder to clear: there is more to remove, and pieces get left behind. **Both** treatments succeed less often on large stones.
:::

::: {.block .example data-title="Size changes the choice"}
Open surgery is the bigger operation (large incision, longer recovery), so doctors kept it mostly for **large** stones and sent small ones to keyhole.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.block .alert data-title="Keep this in mind"}
Stone size is settled **before** the doctor chooses, and it pushes on **both** the treatment and the outcome. If A got more of the hard cases, its overall success rate reflects its cases, not just how well it works.
:::

::: {.notes}
Students rarely know anything about kidney stones, and they do not need much. Many stones pass on their own; these 700 patients needed theirs removed. Three facts carry the whole example. First, the study split patients at a stone diameter of 2 cm: 357 had small stones, 343 had large ones. The picture is to scale: the small stone fits inside the 2 cm circle, the large one spills out of it. Second, large stones are harder for any treatment, because there is more material to remove and pieces get left behind. Third, open surgery is the bigger operation, so doctors reserved it mostly for the large stones, and the newer keyhole procedure got mostly the easier, small ones. Put the second and third facts together and you have the whole puzzle: A was handed the hard cases. Ask the room to predict what that does to A's overall success rate; the Simpson's paradox slide puts numbers on it. A subtle point for later: "large" lumps together a 2.1 cm stone and a 5 cm one, so the two-group split is a coarse summary of size. Some differences in difficulty could remain inside each group, which is one reason the deck later asks how sensitive the answer is to things we did not measure.
:::

# Foundations {#foundations .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[From *what we observe* to *what we wish we knew*.]{.section-subtitle}

```{=html}
<div class="pipeline"><div class="on"><b>1 · Question</b></div><div><b>2 · Estimand</b></div><div><b>3 · Identification</b></div><div><b>4 · Estimation</b></div><div><b>5 · Uncertainty</b></div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
This section is about stage 1: asking the right question. We start by writing the problem down as random variables, so every later question has a precise form. The main lesson is that "do patients who got A do better?" and "would patients do better if we gave them A?" are different questions, and that the data alone cannot tell you which one you have answered.
:::

## The problem as random variables {data-menu-title="Random variables"}

Each patient $i$ gives us three random variables, listed in the order they happen:

::: {.compact style="font-size: 1.12em"}
| Variable | Values | When it is settled |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $X$ = stone size | small, large | **First**: the patient arrives with it |
| $T$ = treatment | $1$ = A (open), $0$ = B (keyhole) | **Second**: the doctor chooses, having seen $X$ |
| $Y$ = outcome | $1$ = success, $0$ = failure | **Last**: after the treatment |
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
**The data** are 700 rows, one per patient, such as $(X_1, T_1, Y_1) = (\text{large}, 1, 1)$.

Each row is an independent draw from one joint distribution $P(X, T, Y)$.
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.block .example data-title="The running example, in symbols"}
- $P(Y{=}1 \mid T{=}1) = 273/350 = 78.0\,\%$ (A's patients)
- $P(Y{=}1 \mid T{=}0) = 289/350 = 82.6\,\%$ (B's patients)
- $P(X{=}\text{large}) = 343/700 = 49\,\%$ (all patients)

[We read each probability off as a proportion of the 700 patients; how precise these are is a Section 4 question.]{.small .muted}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This slide answers "what exactly is our data?" before we ask anything clever of it. There are only three variables, and their order in time matters: the stone comes first, the doctor's choice second, the outcome last. Coding T as 1 for A and 0 for B is a convention; nothing changes if you flip it, except the sign of the effects. The example row shows the shape of the data set (one row per patient); it is not a real patient record, since the study published only counts, but every combination of the three variables occurs in it. The "independent draws from one joint distribution" sentence is the standard statistical model: the patients are a sample, and P(X, T, Y) describes the population they come from. Every number students saw on the running-example slide is a probability about these three variables, as the box shows. For now we treat the sample proportions as if they were the probabilities; sampling uncertainty comes in Section 4, where we put confidence intervals on everything.
:::

## Each patient's story, as probabilities {data-menu-title="The story as probabilities"}

The chain rule lets us write the joint distribution in the order things happen:

$$
P(x, t, y) \;=\; \underbrace{P(x)}_{\text{stone size}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\color{#d1495b}{P(t \mid x)}}_{\text{the doctor's choice}} \;\times\; \underbrace{P(y \mid t, x)}_{\text{the outcome}}
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.block data-title="P(x): who walks in"}
51 % small stones, 49 % large.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="34%"}
::: {.block data-title="P(t | x): who gets what"}
The doctors' rule: large stones went mostly to A.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.block data-title="P(y | t, x): what happens"}
Chance of success for each treatment and size.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.block .alert data-title="The question, stated precisely"}
The overall rates $P(Y{=}1 \mid T{=}t)$ mix in the doctors' habits. Our question: what if **we** chose the treatment? Keep $P(x)$ and $P(y \mid t, x)$, replace $P(t \mid x)$ with "everyone gets A" (or B). The next slide gives this a symbol.
:::

[This assumes stone size is all that drove both the choice and the outcome; Section 2 names the assumption.]{.tiny .muted}

::: {.notes}
The chain rule of probability allows any ordering of the variables; we pick the order in which things actually happen, because then each factor has a physical meaning. Read the three boxes left to right as one patient's story: nature hands them a stone, the doctor picks a treatment after seeing it, and the treatment then succeeds or fails with a probability that depends on both. The middle factor, in red, is the troublemaker. It is the only part of the story that belongs to the doctors rather than to the disease or the treatment, and it is exactly what would change if we ran a different policy. The overall success rate of A mixes in the middle factor because it averages A's success over the patients doctors chose for A, who were mostly large stones. The causal question keeps the first and last factors and swaps out the middle one. That is all an intervention is, and the next slide introduces Pearl's notation for it, do(T = 1). Section 3 comes back to this exact factorization as graph surgery. Caveat for sharp students: the last factor measures how the treatment works only if nothing other than stone size influenced both the choice and the outcome. If doctors also looked at, say, the patient's frailty, then P(y | t, x) mixes the treatment with frailty too. That assumption gets its name, conditional ignorability, in Section 2.
:::

## Seeing versus doing

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block data-title="Seeing (conditioning)"}
Look at the patients who **happened to** get A. What fraction succeeded?

$$\mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid T = 1) = 78\,\%$$

Who got A was decided by doctors, so this group may differ from the B group in many ways besides the treatment.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block .example data-title="Doing (intervening)"}
Imagine **we** give A to *every* patient. What fraction would succeed?

$$\mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid \operatorname{do}(T = 1)) = \ ?$$

Same 700 patients, same mix of cases. Only the doctors' rule for choosing is replaced by "everyone gets A"; if stone size is all that drove their choice, $P(x)$ and $P(y \mid t, x)$ stay as they were.
:::
:::
::::

[Seeing describes the world as it is. Doing asks what would happen if we changed one thing. They are different questions, and usually they have different answers.]{.big}

::: {.notes}
This is the single most important distinction in the deck. The symbol do(T = 1) was introduced by Judea Pearl; read it as "set T to 1 for everyone, by intervention". Conditioning on T = 1 means "restrict attention to the people for whom T happened to be 1". If doctors gave A to the sickest patients, then the "seeing" number mixes the effect of A with the effect of being sick. The question mark on the right is deliberate: by the end of this section we will have a number for it.
:::

## Association is not causation, formally {data-menu-title="Association vs causation"}

- An **association** is a property of $P(Y \mid T)$: how the distribution of $Y$ differs *between the groups* that happened to receive different treatments.
- A **causal effect** is a property of $P(Y \mid \operatorname{do}(T))$: how $Y$ would change if we *set* $T$ ourselves. (Section 2 gives an equivalent definition with potential outcomes.)
- In general $P(y \mid t) \neq P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t))$. They differ whenever something affects **both** the treatment and the outcome, like a patient's condition affecting both the doctor's choice and the chance of success.

::: {.block .alert data-title="Guiding principle"}
The data alone can never tell you which of the two you are looking at. To draw causal conclusions you need causal assumptions about how the data were generated: *"no causes in, no causes out"* (Cartwright, 1989; a theme of Pearl's work).
:::

::: {.notes}
Students often ask: "With enough data, can't we just learn the causal effect?" No. Two completely different causal stories can produce exactly the same joint distribution of (T, Y, X), and then no amount of data can tell them apart. The assumptions must come from outside the data: from knowledge of how treatments were assigned, from biology, from the design of the study. The rest of the deck is about stating those assumptions explicitly, using them correctly, and checking how much the conclusions depend on them.
:::

## The ladder of causation (Pearl)

::: {.compact}
| Rung | Question | Kidney-stone version | Object |
|:-----|:---------|:---------------------|:------:|
| 1. Association (*seeing*) | What do we observe together? | Among patients who got A, what fraction succeeded? | $P(y \mid t)$ |
| 2. Intervention (*doing*) | What if I act? | If we gave A to everyone, what fraction would succeed? | $P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t))$ |
| 3. Counterfactual (*imagining*) | What would have happened? | This patient got B and it failed. Would A have worked for *them*? | $P(y_t \mid t', y')$ |
:::

- $y_t$ is Pearl's notation for "the value $Y$ would have taken had $T$ been $t$", the **potential outcome**. From Section 2 on we write it $Y(t)$. Here $t'$ and $y'$ are what actually happened.
- Each rung needs information the rung below cannot supply. Observational data alone do not answer rung 2; even a perfect experiment does not answer rung 3 for an individual patient.

[This three-row table is the whole course in miniature: most of the deck lives on rung 2.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
Rung 1 is ordinary statistics and machine learning: prediction from patterns. Rung 2 is about policies: what happens if we give everyone A. Rung 3 is about a specific individual and a world that did not happen: this patient, who failed on B, would they have succeeded on A? Rung 3 is harder because the same experiment result is compatible with many individual-level stories. Example: if A cures half the patients, it could cure a fixed half every time, or act randomly. We come back to rung 3 briefly in the causal-graphs section.
:::

## Simpson's paradox: the full table {data-menu-title="Simpson's paradox"}

|               | Small stones (< 2 cm) | Large stones (≥ 2 cm) | All patients |
|:--------------|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|
| A (open) | 81/87 = **93.1 %** | 192/263 = **73.0 %** | 273/350 = 78.0 % |
| B (keyhole) | 234/270 = 86.7 % | 55/80 = 68.75 % | 289/350 = **82.6 %** |
| **A − B** | **+6.4 pp** | **+4.3 pp** | −4.6 pp |

- A wins for small stones **and** for large stones, yet B wins overall. This reversal is called **Simpson's paradox**.
- **Why?** As we saw, large stones are harder to treat (about 70 % success versus about 90 %), and doctors gave the more invasive surgery, A, mostly to large stones: **75 %** of A's patients had large stones, versus **23 %** of B's.\
  In symbols: $P(X{=}\text{large} \mid T{=}1) = 0.75$ but $P(X{=}\text{large} \mid T{=}0) = 0.23$.
- So the overall comparison pits *A on mostly hard cases* against *B on mostly easy cases*. Stone size affects both the treatment choice and the outcome. A variable like that is called a **confounder**.

::: {.notes}
Reveal this slowly. First show the "All patients" column, which students already saw. Then show the two stone-size columns. Let the reversal sink in. Then explain the mechanism with the two percentages: 263 out of 350 A patients had large stones (75 %), only 80 out of 350 B patients did (23 %). The "pp" means percentage points, the difference between two percentages. There is nothing wrong with the arithmetic; the paradox comes from comparing groups that differ in difficulty. Likely question: "Is this a rare curiosity?" No. Any time treatment choice depends on something that also affects the outcome, the aggregate comparison can be biased, and sometimes, as here, even the sign flips.
:::

## Simpson's paradox, live {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{ojs}
viewof pA = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 263/350, step: 0.001, label: "Share of large stones among A's patients"})
viewof pB = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 80/350, step: 0.001, label: "Share of large stones among B's patients"})
```

```{ojs}
simpsonRows = {
  const r = {A: {peq: 81/87, gra: 192/263}, B: {peq: 234/270, gra: 55/80}};
  const tot = (k, p) => (1 - p) * r[k].peq + p * r[k].gra;
  return [
    {grupo: "Small", trat: "A", tasa: r.A.peq}, {grupo: "Small", trat: "B", tasa: r.B.peq},
    {grupo: "Large", trat: "A", tasa: r.A.gra}, {grupo: "Large", trat: "B", tasa: r.B.gra},
    {grupo: "All patients", trat: "A", tasa: tot("A", pA)}, {grupo: "All patients", trat: "B", tasa: tot("B", pB)}
  ];
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 620, height: 300, marginTop: 30, marginLeft: 48,
  fx: {domain: ["Small", "Large", "All patients"], label: null},
  x: {axis: null, domain: ["A", "B"]},
  y: {domain: [0, 1.08], label: "Success rate", tickFormat: "%", grid: true},
  color: {domain: ["A", "B"], range: ["#14213d", "#c8742b"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(simpsonRows, {fx: "grupo", x: "trat", y: "tasa", fill: "trat"}),
    Plot.text(simpsonRows, {fx: "grupo", x: "trat", y: "tasa", text: d => (100 * d.tasa).toFixed(0) + "%", dy: -9, fontSize: 13})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{ojs}
{
  const a = simpsonRows[4].tasa, b = simpsonRows[5].tasa;
  return html`<div class="readout">
    All patients: A = <b>${(100*a).toFixed(1)}%</b>, B = <b>${(100*b).toFixed(1)}%</b><br>
    ${a < b ? "⚠️ <b>Paradox:</b> B 'wins' overall although A wins for both stone sizes, because A got more of the hard cases."
            : "✓ Now the overall comparison agrees with the comparison within each stone size: A wins."}
  </div>`;
}
```

The bars for small and large stones **never move**: the treatments work exactly as well as before. The sliders change only **who gets which cases**.

**Try this:**

1. Drag A's share of large stones down to B's level (0.23). The paradox disappears.
2. Type **0.49** into **both** boxes: the share of large stones among all 700 patients. You get A = 83.3 %, B = 77.9 %: the fair comparison of the next slide.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Drive the widget live. The starting position is the real study: 75 % of A's patients had large stones, 23 % of B's. Step 1: move A's slider down toward 0.23; at some point the overall bars cross and A wins. Step 2: put both sliders at 0.49, the population share of large stones (343 out of 700). Now both treatments are evaluated on the same case mix, and the overall rates are exactly the standardized rates we compute by hand on the next slide. Key message: the overall comparison mixes two things, the effect of the treatment and the effect of the case mix. Fixing the case mix isolates the treatment.
:::

## Comparing like with like: standardization {data-menu-title="Standardization"}

**Idea:** compare A and B *within* each stone size, then average using the **whole population's** size mix.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{A: } & 0.51 \times 93.1\,\% + 0.49 \times 73.0\,\% = 83.3\,\% \\
\text{B: } & 0.51 \times 86.7\,\% + 0.49 \times 68.75\,\% = 77.9\,\%
\end{aligned}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \text{A} - \text{B} = \mathbf{+5.4} \text{ pp}
$$

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
p_size <- c(small = 357, large = 343) / 700   # stone-size mix of all 700 patients
rate_A <- c(small = 81/87,   large = 192/263)  # success rate of A within each size
rate_B <- c(small = 234/270, large = 55/80)    # success rate of B within each size
sum(p_size * rate_A) - sum(p_size * rate_B)    # 0.054: A is better by about 5 points
```

### Python

```python
p_size = {"small": 357 / 700, "large": 343 / 700}  # stone-size mix of all 700 patients
rate_A = {"small": 81 / 87, "large": 192 / 263}    # success rate of A within each size
rate_B = {"small": 234 / 270, "large": 55 / 80}    # success rate of B within each size
sum(p_size[s] * (rate_A[s] - rate_B[s]) for s in p_size)   # 0.054
```
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
So $\mathbb{P}(Y{=}1 \mid \operatorname{do}(T{=}1)) \approx 83.3\,\%$, the "?" from *Seeing versus doing*. You will meet this formula again as the identification formula (Section 2) and the backdoor adjustment formula, or g-formula (Section 3); g-computation and IPW (Section 4) are two ways to estimate it.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is our first adjustment formula, and it answers the "doing" question from earlier: the question mark in P(Y = 1 | do(T = 1)) is about 83.3 %, provided stone size is the only thing that drove both the choice and the outcome. That proviso is an assumption, and Section 2 gives it a name (conditional ignorability). Point out that the weights are the population shares 0.51 and 0.49 (357 small and 343 large stones out of 700), not the shares within each treatment group; using each group's own mix is exactly what produced the misleading 78 % versus 82.6 %. The adjusted effect is +5.4 percentage points in favor of A. Students will meet this formula again under other names: the identification formula (Section 2) and the backdoor adjustment formula, also called the g-formula (Section 3). g-computation and inverse probability weighting (Section 4) are not new formulas but two different ways to estimate this same quantity when there are many covariates.
:::

## So which number is right? Ask the story, not the table {data-menu-title="Which number is right?"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block .example data-title="Story 1: stone size"}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 150" width="100%" height="140" style="font-family:'Source Sans 3',sans-serif;font-size:17px">
  <defs><marker id="fdArrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#14213d"/></marker></defs>
  <g fill="none" stroke="#14213d" stroke-width="2">
    <rect x="100" y="8" width="160" height="34" rx="17"/>
    <rect x="15" y="105" width="110" height="34" rx="17"/><rect x="235" y="105" width="110" height="34" rx="17"/>
    <line x1="140" y1="42" x2="92" y2="102" marker-end="url(#fdArrow)"/>
    <line x1="220" y1="42" x2="268" y2="102" marker-end="url(#fdArrow)"/>
    <line x1="125" y1="122" x2="231" y2="122" marker-end="url(#fdArrow)"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="#14213d" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="central">
    <text x="180" y="25">Stone size</text><text x="70" y="122">Treatment</text><text x="290" y="122">Success</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```
Size is decided **before** treatment and drives both the choice and the outcome. **Compare within sizes**: A is better by 5.4 pp.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block .example data-title="Story 2: same numbers, different variable"}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 150" width="100%" height="140" style="font-family:'Source Sans 3',sans-serif;font-size:17px">
  <g fill="none" stroke="#14213d" stroke-width="2">
    <rect x="100" y="8" width="160" height="34" rx="17"/>
    <rect x="15" y="105" width="110" height="34" rx="17"/><rect x="235" y="105" width="110" height="34" rx="17"/>
    <line x1="92" y1="102" x2="140" y2="45" marker-end="url(#fdArrow)"/>
    <line x1="220" y1="42" x2="268" y2="102" marker-end="url(#fdArrow)"/>
    <line x1="125" y1="122" x2="231" y2="122" marker-end="url(#fdArrow)"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="#14213d" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="central">
    <text x="180" y="25">Blood pressure</text><text x="70" y="122">Treatment</text><text x="290" y="122">Success</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```
Suppose the column split were *post-operative blood pressure*, **caused by** the treatment. Splitting on it hides part of the effect. **Use the overall comparison** (if nothing else drove the choice).
:::
:::
::::

::: {.block .alert data-title="The lesson"}
The same table can call for opposite decisions. The numbers cannot tell you whether to adjust; **the causal story can**. Section 3 turns these stories into graphs and gives exact rules.
:::

::: {.notes}
This example is due to Judea Pearl. Imagine the identical table, but the column label is "blood pressure after the operation: low or high" instead of "stone size". The arithmetic does not change at all, yet the right answer does. Stone size exists before treatment and influences it, so it is a confounder and we should stratify on it. Blood pressure after the operation is a consequence of the treatment and part of the route by which the treatment works (a mediator); stratifying on it would compare patients in whom the treatment already did part of its job, which removes part of the effect we want to measure. The arrows in each picture are the causal story. Students should leave this slide convinced that "adjust for everything" is not a safe rule.
:::

## Recap: Foundations {.recap}

- **Seeing** ($P(y \mid t)$) and **doing** ($P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t))$) are different questions: doing replaces how the doctors chose the treatment with our own choice.
- Pearl's ladder: association → intervention → counterfactual. Each rung needs more than the data from the rung below.
- **Simpson's paradox**: B looked 4.6 pp better overall only because A got the hard cases. Within each stone size, A wins.
- **Standardization**, comparing within strata and averaging over the population, gives **+5.4 pp for A**. It is our first adjustment formula.
- Whether to adjust for a variable is decided by the **causal story**, not by the numbers.

[**Test yourself:** Hospital 1 has a higher death rate than Hospital 2 overall, but a lower death rate among mild cases *and* among severe cases. Which hospital would you rather go to, and why?]{.small}

::: {.notes}
Pause for questions here. If students remember one thing, it should be the last bullet: causal conclusions require causal assumptions. Test-yourself answer: Hospital 1. It must treat a much larger share of severe cases, so its overall rate mixes quality of care with case mix. Severity exists before admission and drives both which hospital a patient ends up in and the chance of death, so it is a confounder: compare within severity, where Hospital 1 is better for both. Next we make "the effect of A" precise using potential outcomes, which will also tell us exactly which assumptions justified the standardization we just did.
:::

# Potential Outcomes {#potential-outcomes .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Every causal effect compares two worlds — and we only ever see one.]{.section-subtitle}

```{=html}
<div class="pipeline"><div><b>1 · Question</b></div><div class="on"><b>2 · Estimand</b></div><div class="on"><b>3 · Identification</b></div><div><b>4 · Estimation</b></div><div><b>5 · Uncertainty</b></div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
This section gives us a precise language for "what would have happened". First we define the target (the estimand), then we ask what assumptions let us compute it from data (identification). The key idea of the whole section: every causal question is a comparison between two worlds, and the data only ever show us one of them.
:::

## Two worlds for every patient

Suppose we could see every patient's outcome under **both** treatments (1 = success, 0 = failure).

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.compact style="font-size: 1.15em"}
| Patient | Stone | $Y_i(1)$: if given A | $Y_i(0)$: if given B | $\tau_i$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 1 | small | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 2 | small | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | small | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 4 | small | 1 | 0 | **1** |
| 5 | large | 1 | 0 | **1** |
| 6 | large | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 7 | large | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | large | 1 | 0 | **1** |
| **Average** | | **0.75** | **0.375** | **0.375** |
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
- $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ is patient $i$'s **individual causal effect**. A rescues patients 4, 5 and 8; for the other five it makes no difference.
- If **everyone** got A, 75 % would succeed; if everyone got B, 37.5 %.
- The **average treatment effect** is the average of the last column: **ATE = 0.375**. A raises the success rate by 37.5 percentage points.

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
A causal effect compares two "what-ifs" for the **same** people.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This is a god's-eye view: no real dataset ever looks like this. Each patient carries two potential outcomes — think of them as two sealed envelopes, one for each treatment. The individual effect is the difference between the envelopes. The ATE is just the average of the last column, or equivalently the difference between the two column averages. Keep this table in mind; we will keep coming back to it. Likely question: "Are potential outcomes random?" Here we treat them as fixed properties of each patient; the randomness comes from who gets which treatment.
:::

## What we actually see

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.compact style="font-size: 1.25em"}
| Patient | Stone | Got | $Y_i(1)$ | $Y_i(0)$ | Observed $Y_i$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 1 | small | B | [?]{.q} | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | small | B | [?]{.q} | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | small | B | [?]{.q} | 1 | 1 |
| 4 | small | A | 1 | [?]{.q} | 1 |
| 5 | large | A | 1 | [?]{.q} | 1 |
| 6 | large | A | 0 | [?]{.q} | 0 |
| 7 | large | A | 0 | [?]{.q} | 0 |
| 8 | large | B | [?]{.q} | 0 | 0 |
:::
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
- Each patient receives **one** treatment, so we see **one** potential outcome. The other is missing — forever.
- Naive comparison of the observed groups: A succeeds 2/4 = 50 %, B succeeds 3/4 = 75 %. Difference: **−0.25**.
- A looks **harmful**, yet the truth is **+0.375**. Same patients, opposite conclusion.
- Why? A went to 3 of the 4 large-stone patients — the hard cases.
:::
::::

::: {.block .alert data-title="The fundamental problem of causal inference"}
We can never observe both $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ for the same unit. Causal inference is a **missing-data problem**: every method in this deck is a disciplined way of filling in the [?]{.q} cells.
:::

::: {.notes}
Now the realistic view: the same eight patients, but we only see the outcome of the treatment each one actually got. Half the table is question marks. The naive comparison gets the sign wrong, for exactly the reason we saw with the real kidney-stone data: treatment A was given to the harder cases. Emphasize: nothing is wrong with the arithmetic; the comparison itself is unfair because the two groups were different before treatment. Ask the room: which question marks would you need to fill in to get the right answer? (All of them, or at least their averages.)
:::

## The Neyman–Rubin framework

::: {.block data-title="Definition 1 (Potential outcomes · Neyman 1923, Rubin 1974)"}
For each unit $i$ and binary treatment $T_i \in \{0, 1\}$, the **potential outcomes** $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ are the outcomes unit $i$ would have under treatment and under control. They are fixed attributes of the unit, defined before treatment is assigned.
:::

::: {.block data-title="Consistency: from potential outcomes to data"}
The observed outcome is the potential outcome of the treatment actually received:
$$Y_i = T_i\, Y_i(1) + (1 - T_i)\, Y_i(0).$$
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
The equation is bookkeeping: if $T_i = 1$ it reads $Y_i = Y_i(1)$; if $T_i = 0$ it reads $Y_i = Y_i(0)$. Only one term survives, so $\tau_i$ can never be computed from data — we aim at **averages** instead.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide just writes the previous two slides in symbols. Neyman introduced potential outcomes for randomized experiments in 1923; Rubin extended the framework to observational studies in 1974, which is why it is often called the Rubin causal model. Potential outcomes come first and exist for everyone; the treatment then decides which one gets revealed. The consistency equation is the only link between the potential outcomes and the data, and it is used in every proof in this section. The punchline: individual effects are out of reach, but averages over groups can be recovered under assumptions — that is what the rest of the section is about.
:::

## Causal estimands: what exactly do we want?

An **estimand** is the precise quantity we are after. Different questions call for different averages of $\tau_i$:

::: {.compact style="font-size: 1.1em"}
| Estimand | Definition | The question it answers | Toy table | Kidney stones |
|:----|:------------|:-------------|:------:|:--------:|
| ATE | $\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)]$ | What if *everyone* got A instead of B? | 0.375 | +5.4 pp |
| ATT | $\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 1]$ | Did A help the patients who *actually got* A? | 0.5 | +4.8 pp |
| ATC | $\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 0]$ | Would A have helped those who got B? | 0.25 | +5.9 pp |
| CATE$(x)$ | $\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]$ | What is the effect for patients *like this one*? | small 0.25, large 0.5 | small +6.4, large +4.3 |
:::

- The pieces fit together: $\text{ATE} = \mathbb{P}(T=1)\,\text{ATT} + \mathbb{P}(T=0)\,\text{ATC}$. Toy table: 0.5 × 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.375.
- Choose the **estimand before the estimator**: "give A to everyone?" needs the ATE; "was the program worth it for those enrolled?" needs the ATT.

[Kidney-stone values are estimates that assume stone size is the only confounder — we justify that assumption later in this section.]{.tiny .muted}

::: {.notes}
"pp" means percentage points. Walk through the four questions in words before looking at the formulas — each formula is just "average of tau over a particular group". Toy numbers: ATT averages tau over patients 4 to 7, ATC over patients 1, 2, 3 and 8, and CATE over small-stone patients (1 to 4) or large-stone patients (5 to 8). The ATE identity is just the law of total expectation. Effects can also be expressed on other scales, such as the risk ratio E[Y(1)]/E[Y(0)] (2.0 in the toy table) or as differences in quantiles; the choice of scale is part of choosing the estimand.
:::

## SUTVA: a treatment must mean one thing, for one person

Writing $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ already assumes each patient has exactly **two** possible outcomes.

::: {.block data-title="Definition 2 (SUTVA: stable unit treatment value assumption)"}
**(i) No interference**: $Y_i$ depends only on $T_i$, not on other units' treatments $T_j$. **(ii) No hidden versions**: each treatment comes in only one version.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**When (i) fails — spillovers**

- Vaccines: my vaccination protects you too.
- Tutoring: treated students help untreated classmates.
- Then $Y_i$ depends on everyone's treatment: we need *direct* and *spillover* effects.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**When (ii) fails — versions**

- "Open surgery" by an experienced surgeon vs. a trainee.
- "Exercise": a daily walk or marathon training?
- Then "the effect of A" is ambiguous: define the treatment precisely.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SUTVA is easy to skip past, but without it the notation does not even make sense: if your outcome depends on your roommate's vaccination, you do not have just two potential outcomes, you have one for every combination of treatments in your network. For the kidney stones, SUTVA is plausible: one patient's surgery does not change another patient's result, as long as "open surgery" means roughly the same procedure everywhere. Ask: can you think of a treatment in your field where spillovers are the whole point? (Advertising, policing, vaccination, and anything spreading through social networks.)
:::

## The naive comparison = effect + selection bias

Start from the naive difference, replace $Y$ by potential outcomes (consistency), then add and subtract $\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=1]$:

::: {style="font-size: 0.88em"}
$$
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=0]}_{\text{naive difference}}
= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T=1]}_{\text{ATT: the effect}}
+ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=0]}_{\text{selection bias}}
$$
:::

::: {.block .example data-title="Running example: the 8-patient table — naive −0.25 = ATT 0.5 + bias (−0.75)"}
- **ATT = 0.5**: among A's patients (4–7), A rescued 2 of 4.
- **Selection bias = 0 − 0.75 = −0.75**: *without* treatment, A's patients would have succeeded 0 of 4 times; B's patients 3 of 4 times.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
The naive difference mixes the effect of the treatment with **how different the groups were to begin with**. Here B got the easy cases, and that head start (−0.75) swamps A's real benefit (+0.5).
:::

::: {.notes}
This decomposition is the most useful identity in the section; it holds exactly, in any dataset, with no assumptions beyond consistency. Do the add-and-subtract step on the board if there is time: E[Y | T=1] is E[Y(1) | T=1] by consistency, E[Y | T=0] is E[Y(0) | T=0]; adding and subtracting E[Y(0) | T=1] splits the difference into the ATT and the bias. The selection-bias term asks: how different would the two groups be if nobody were treated? It can be positive or negative. The next slide lets you control its sign.
:::

## Selection bias, live {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{ojs}
viewof kSel = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Selection on X (k)"})
viewof aleat = Inputs.toggle({label: "Randomize T", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
selRes = {
  const rng = mulberry32(42), n = 20000;
  let s1 = 0, s0 = 0, n1 = 0, n0 = 0, y01 = 0, y00 = 0, att = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const x = randn(rng);
    const t = aleat ? (rng() < 0.5 ? 1 : 0) : (kSel * x + randn(rng) > 0 ? 1 : 0);
    const y0 = x + randn(rng), y1 = y0 + 1;   // true effect = 1
    if (t) { n1++; s1 += y1; y01 += y0; att += y1 - y0; } else { n0++; s0 += y0; y00 += y0; }
  }
  const naive = s1 / n1 - s0 / n0, sesgo = y01 / n1 - y00 / n0;
  return [
    {termino: "Naive difference", valor: naive},
    {termino: "ATT (effect)", valor: att / n1},
    {termino: "Selection bias", valor: sesgo}
  ];
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 210, marginLeft: 150,
  marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [-2, 3], label: "Value", grid: true, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36},
  y: {label: null, domain: selRes.map(d => d.termino)},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(selRes, {y: "termino", x: "valor", fill: d => d.termino.startsWith("ATT") ? "#2e8b57" : d.termino.startsWith("Selection") ? "#c8742b" : "#14213d"}),
    Plot.text(selRes, {y: "termino", x: "valor", text: d => (Math.abs(d.valor) < 0.005 ? 0 : d.valor).toFixed(2), dx: 22}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

[Simulated data, $n = 20\,000$: $Y(0) = X + \varepsilon$, $Y(1) = Y(0) + 1$ (true effect 1 for everyone), $T = \mathbb{1}\{kX + \eta > 0\}$, with $X, \varepsilon, \eta \sim N(0, 1)$.]{.small}
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
**$k$ controls who gets treated.** Units with high $X$ also have high $Y(0)$ — they would do well anyway.

**Three things to try**

1. $k = 1$: high-$X$ units get treated, so the bias is **positive** and the naive difference overstates the effect.
2. $k = -1$: the bias flips sign; the naive difference understates it. **Kidney stones are this case**: A went to patients with worse $Y(0)$ (large stones), so the naive comparison understates A's effect.
3. Switch on **Randomize T**: the bias vanishes for every $k$, and the naive difference recovers the true effect of 1.

Check the identity on the bars: naive = ATT + bias.

```r
naive <- mean(Y[T == 1]) - mean(Y[T == 0])
# the bias needs Y0 for everyone: simulation only
bias  <- mean(Y0[T == 1]) - mean(Y0[T == 0])
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The slider k is how strongly treatment assignment depends on X. Because X also drives the outcome, k effectively decides whether the treated group is "already better off" (k > 0) or "already worse off" (k < 0). The effect itself never changes: it is always 1. Only the bias moves. The kidney stones sit on the negative side: A was given to the harder cases, so its naive comparison (−4.6 pp) understates the adjusted effect (+5.4 pp). Point out the comment in the code: we can compute the bias here only because a simulation lets us see Y(0) for everyone. In real data the bias term is invisible, which is why we need either randomization or assumptions.
:::

## Why randomization works

**Intuition**: a coin flip cannot know your potential outcomes. So the treated and control groups are, on average, alike in **everything** — stone size, frailty, genes, things nobody measured.

::: {.block data-title="Randomization"}
If $T$ is assigned by a coin, then $T \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1))$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=1] = \mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=0]$, so the **selection bias is zero**, and also $\text{ATT} = \text{ATE}$:
$$\mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=0] = \text{ATE}.$$
:::

::: {.block .example data-title="Running example: kidney stones"}
Had a coin chosen between A and B, both groups would contain (on average) the same share of large stones. No Simpson's paradox — the plain comparison would be fair.
:::

[Here $\perp\!\!\!\perp$ means "is independent of". This is why randomized controlled trials are the gold standard: they balance **unmeasured** confounders too. Balance holds on average; in a small trial chance imbalances remain, which is what standard errors account for.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
Connect this to the decomposition on the previous slides: randomization kills the selection-bias term, and because the treated group is a random half of everyone, the ATT equals the ATE. Stress "on average": in any single small experiment the groups can differ by chance, and that chance is exactly what confidence intervals quantify. Common question: does randomization require equal group sizes? No — any known assignment probability works, and it can even depend on measured covariates (stratified or blocked designs).
:::

## Analyzing a randomized experiment

- **Neyman's estimator** $\hat\tau = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0$: the difference of the two group means. With a fixed number of treated patients (*complete randomization*), its average over all possible coin flips is exactly the ATE: it is **unbiased**.
- **Its variance** is estimated by $\hat V = \dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_0^2}{n_0}$, where $s_t^2$ is the sample variance and $n_t$ the size of group $t$. It is **conservative** (a little too large): the true variance also depends on how $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ co-vary, which we never observe.
- **95 % confidence interval**: $\hat\tau \pm 1.96\,\sqrt{\hat V}$, by the central limit theorem.

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Randomization makes the simplest comparison the right one. What is left is **noise**: how much would the difference move if the coins had landed differently? The variance formula answers that, erring on the safe side.
:::

::: {.notes}
Each bullet is one idea. Neyman: the randomness is in the assignment, not in the potential outcomes; unbiasedness is an average over re-randomizations of the same patients. Conservative variance: we never see Y(1) and Y(0) together, so we cannot estimate their correlation; the formula assumes the worst case and is exact when the effect is the same for everyone. Because the variance estimate is too large rather than too small, the 95 % interval covers the ATE at least 95 % of the time in large samples. The next slide adds two refinements that are worth knowing but not essential on a first pass.
:::

## Two refinements: Fisher's test and Lin's adjustment {.deeper}

::: {.block data-title="Fisher's exact test (the sharp null)"}
Suppose the treatment did *nothing* for *anyone*: $Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)$ for every $i$. Then every [?]{.q} cell is known — it equals the observed outcome! So we can reshuffle $T$ thousands of times, recompute $\hat\tau$ each time, and ask how unusual the real $\hat\tau$ is. The p-value is the share of reshuffles at least as extreme. It is exact, even with ten patients.
:::

::: {.block data-title="Covariate adjustment (Lin, 2013)"}
Regress $Y$ on $T$, the **pre-treatment** covariates (centered at their means), and their interactions with $T$; use robust (HC2) standard errors. The coefficient on $T$ still targets the ATE, usually with a smaller standard error, and in large samples it is never less precise than the plain difference in means.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Fisher tests "no effect for anyone" without any large-sample approximation. Lin borrows precision from covariates: they soak up outcome noise, but in an experiment they are not needed to remove bias.
:::

::: {.notes}
Fisher: the beautiful trick is that under the sharp null the missing column is filled in by the observed one, so we can compute the exact distribution of the estimator under re-randomization. Note what it tests: no effect for anyone, which is stronger than "average effect zero". Lin: adjustment does not fix bias in an experiment (there is none); it soaks up outcome variation and makes the estimate more precise. Centering matters: with centered covariates the coefficient on T is the ATE rather than the effect at X = 0. Covariates must be measured before treatment, or adjustment can introduce bias.
:::

## In code: analyzing an experiment {.deeper}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
tau_hat <- mean(Y[T == 1]) - mean(Y[T == 0])                 # Neyman estimator
V_hat   <- var(Y[T == 1]) / sum(T) + var(Y[T == 0]) / sum(1 - T)
tau_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(V_hat)              # 95% confidence interval

# Fisher's exact test, approximated by permutation under the sharp null
perm <- replicate(10000, { Tp <- sample(T); mean(Y[Tp == 1]) - mean(Y[Tp == 0]) })
mean(abs(perm) >= abs(tau_hat))                               # p-value

# Lin (2013): interactions with centered covariates + robust (HC2) standard errors
Xc  <- scale(X, scale = FALSE)                                # X: matrix of covariates
lin <- lm(Y ~ T * Xc)
coef(lin)["T"]                                                # adjusted estimate of the ATE
sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(lin, type = "HC2")))["T"]          # its standard error
```

### Python

```python
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
diff = lambda t: Y[t == 1].mean() - Y[t == 0].mean()
tau_hat = diff(T)                                              # Neyman estimator
V_hat = Y[T == 1].var(ddof=1) / T.sum() + Y[T == 0].var(ddof=1) / (1 - T).sum()

perm = np.array([diff(rng.permutation(T)) for _ in range(10_000)])
p_fisher = np.mean(np.abs(perm) >= abs(tau_hat))               # permutation p-value

# Lin adjustment: df has columns Y, T, X1, X2
df["X1_c"], df["X2_c"] = df.X1 - df.X1.mean(), df.X2 - df.X2.mean()
lin = smf.ols("Y ~ T * (X1_c + X2_c)", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC2")
print(lin.params["T"], lin.bse["T"])
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Here Y and T are vectors of outcomes and 0/1 treatment indicators. The permutation test re-randomizes the treatment labels: under the sharp null the outcomes would not change, so the reshuffled differences show what chance alone produces. Centering the covariates matters for Lin's estimator: it makes the coefficient on T equal the ATE rather than the effect at X = 0.
:::

## When we cannot randomize: conditional ignorability

**Intuition**: doctors did not flip a coin, but maybe treatment was **as good as random within groups of similar patients** — say, among small-stone patients.

::: {.block data-title="Definition 3 (Conditional ignorability)"}
$$(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid X$$
Within each level of the covariates $X$, treatment is independent of the potential outcomes.
:::

::: {.block .example data-title="Running example: kidney stones"}
With $X$ = stone size: within each size group, A's and B's patients are comparable. **What would break it**: doctors also judging frailty by eye — never recorded — and sending frail patients to the gentler B. Then B's patients are frailer *within* each size group.
:::

[Also called *unconfoundedness* or *no unmeasured confounding*. It **cannot be tested** from data — it is a claim about the [?]{.q} cells — so it must be argued from subject knowledge. Causal graphs (next section) are the tool for that.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
This is the assumption that replaces the coin flip. It says: once you know X, knowing which treatment someone got tells you nothing more about their potential outcomes. A variable that affects both treatment and outcome and is not in X — like unrecorded frailty — breaks it. Stress the honest part: no statistical test can confirm it, because it is a statement about outcomes we never observe. All the observational methods in this deck rest on it (or on a design-based replacement for it, which we meet later).
:::

## Positivity: everyone needs a chance of either treatment

::: {.block data-title="Definition 4 (Positivity, or overlap)"}
$$0 < e(x) < 1 \quad \text{for every } x \text{ that occurs}, \qquad \text{where } e(x) = \mathbb{P}(T = 1 \mid X = x).$$
:::

- $e(x)$ is the **propensity score**: the probability that a unit with covariates $x$ gets treated. It returns in the estimation section.
- Kidney stones: $e(\text{small}) = 87/357 = 0.244$, $e(\text{large}) = 263/343 = 0.767$. Both strictly between 0 and 1 ✓

::: {.block .alert data-title="What goes wrong without it"}
If *every* large-stone patient had received A, we would have **no data at all** on B for large stones. No method can compare A with B in a group where B never happens — it can only extrapolate.
:::

[Unlike ignorability, positivity **can be checked** in the data. Near-violations ($e(x)$ close to 0 or 1) make estimates unstable.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
Positivity is the "you need someone to compare with" assumption. Within every type of patient there must be some who got A and some who got B. A structural violation is a rule like "never operate on anyone over 80". Practical near-violations are more common: if only 1 % of some group got treated, the few treated units carry enormous weight, and the estimate becomes noisy — we will see this vividly with IPW weights in the propensity-score 3D scene.
:::

## Identification: turning a "what-if" into a formula

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 5 (Identifying the ATE)"}
Under SUTVA, conditional ignorability, and positivity,
$$\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}_X\big[\,\mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=1, X) - \mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=0, X)\,\big].$$
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Compare treated and untreated units **within** each group of similar units, then **average** the differences, weighting each group by how common it is. The left side involves unobservable potential outcomes; the right side only observable data. That is what **identification** means.
:::

::: {.block .example data-title="Running example: kidney stones"}
This is exactly the calculation on *Comparing like with like: standardization*: within-size differences of +6.4 and +4.3 pp, weighted by 0.51 and 0.49, give **+5.4 pp**.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff of the section. Once a causal quantity has been written as a function of the distribution of observed data, the rest is a statistics problem: estimate that function well. In pipeline terms, we have moved from stage 2 (the estimand) to stage 3 (identification). Notice which assumption does what: ignorability lets us swap potential outcomes for observed outcomes within strata; positivity guarantees both conditional means exist; SUTVA makes the potential outcomes well defined in the first place. The formula is called standardization, the adjustment formula, or the g-formula; it will reappear as the backdoor formula.
:::

## Why the identification theorem works {.deeper}

::: {.block data-title="Proof, line by line"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y(1)] &= \mathbb{E}_X\big[\mathbb{E}(Y(1) \mid X)\big] && \text{law of iterated expectations} \\
&= \mathbb{E}_X\big[\mathbb{E}(Y(1) \mid T=1, X)\big] && \text{ignorability: given } X, T \text{ says nothing about } Y(1) \\
&= \mathbb{E}_X\big[\mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=1, X)\big] && \text{consistency: among the treated, } Y = Y(1)
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

- **Positivity** is needed in the last line: $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=1, X=x)$ only exists if some units with $X = x$ were treated.
- The same three steps give $\mathbb{E}[Y(0)] = \mathbb{E}_X[\mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=0, X)]$. Subtract the two lines to get the theorem. $\square$
- **SUTVA** works silently throughout: it makes $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ well defined.

::: {.notes}
The proof is three lines, and each line uses exactly one idea, which is worth saying out loud. The trick is in the middle line: we are allowed to add "T = 1" to the conditioning because, given X, treatment carries no information about Y(1). That is the only place the untestable assumption enters. Then consistency turns the unobservable Y(1) into the observable Y, but only among the treated. If students remember one thing: ignorability is what lets us use the treated group's outcomes to stand in for everyone's Y(1), within each X group.
:::

## Check your understanding: which assumption fails?

**1.** A ride-hailing app randomly gives half of its drivers a discount to offer riders. Riders switch to the discounted drivers, so the other drivers lose business.

```{ojs}
viewof poQ1 = Inputs.radio(["SUTVA", "Ignorability", "Positivity"], {value: null})
```
```{ojs}
quiz(poQ1, "SUTVA", {
  "SUTVA": "Untreated drivers' earnings depend on <i>other drivers'</i> discounts: interference, a violation of SUTVA (i).",
  "Ignorability": "The discount was randomized, so ignorability holds. But one driver's discount changes another's earnings: SUTVA.",
  "Positivity": "Every driver had a 50 % chance of the discount, so overlap is fine. The problem is spillover: SUTVA."})
```

**2.** A new drug is never prescribed during pregnancy. We want its effect for all adult patients, pregnant or not.

```{ojs}
viewof poQ2 = Inputs.radio(["SUTVA", "Ignorability", "Positivity"], {value: null})
```
```{ojs}
quiz(poQ2, "Positivity", {
  "SUTVA": "Patients do not affect each other here. The problem is that one group never receives the drug at all.",
  "Ignorability": "Pregnancy is recorded, so we can condition on it. The problem is that for pregnant patients e(x) = 0: positivity fails.",
  "Positivity": "For pregnant patients e(x) = 0: there is no treated patient to compare with, so their effect cannot be estimated without extrapolating."})
```

**3.** Caseworkers enroll the applicants they judge most motivated into a job-training program. Motivation is never recorded.

```{ojs}
viewof poQ3 = Inputs.radio(["SUTVA", "Ignorability", "Positivity"], {value: null})
```
```{ojs}
quiz(poQ3, "Ignorability", {
  "SUTVA": "Trainees do not affect each other here. A hidden factor drives both enrollment and earnings: ignorability.",
  "Ignorability": "Motivation drives both enrollment and later earnings, and it is unmeasured: an unmeasured confounder.",
  "Positivity": "Anyone could be enrolled or not. The problem is that motivation is not in the data: ignorability."})
```

::: {.notes}
Give the room a minute per question, ideally discussing in pairs before clicking. Question 1 is interference: in a marketplace, treating some sellers changes the outcomes of the untreated ones, so the treated-vs-untreated comparison overstates the effect of rolling the discount out to everyone. Question 2 is a structural positivity violation. Question 3 is the classic unmeasured confounder, the job-training version of the unrecorded-frailty story: motivated applicants would earn more anyway, so the naive comparison overstates the program's effect. A good follow-up: which of the three can you detect in the data? Positivity (look at who got treated in each group); the other two need subject-matter knowledge.
:::

## Recap: Potential outcomes {.recap}

- Every unit has two potential outcomes, $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$; we observe one. Causal inference is a **missing-data problem**.
- Pick the **estimand** first — ATE, ATT, ATC or CATE — because each answers a different question.
- Naive difference = **ATT + selection bias**. Randomization makes the bias zero, even for unmeasured factors.
- Without randomization, **SUTVA + conditional ignorability + positivity** identify the ATE: compare within groups of similar units, then average (kidney stones: +5.4 pp).
- Ignorability cannot be tested; positivity can be checked. Next question: **which** covariates $X$ should we condition on? Causal graphs answer it.

[**Test yourself:** in the 8-patient table, which [?]{.q} cells would you need to fill in to compute the ATT — and what is it?]{.small}

::: {.notes}
Read the five lines and pause on the last one: the theory so far says "condition on the right X", but it does not tell us which X is right. Adding the wrong covariate can create bias rather than remove it. That is the job of the next section, on causal graphs.

Test-yourself answer: the ATT averages the effect over the treated patients (4–7, who got A), so we need their missing Y(0) cells — four question marks. Their Y(1) values are observed (1, 1, 0, 0, mean 0.5) and, from the god's-eye table, their Y(0) values are all 0, so ATT = 0.5 − 0 = 0.5.
:::

# Causal Graphs and Structural Models {#causal-graphs .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Draw the story first. The graph tells you what to measure — and what to leave alone.]{.section-subtitle}

```{=html}
<div class="pipeline"><div><b>1 · Question</b></div><div><b>2 · Estimand</b></div><div class="on"><b>3 · Identification</b></div><div><b>4 · Estimation</b></div><div><b>5 · Uncertainty</b></div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
Potential outcomes told us what an effect *is*. This section answers the next question: given my story about how the data were generated, which comparison recovers that effect? The tool is a picture — a causal graph — plus a few rules for reading it. By the end, students should be able to look at a graph and say which variables to adjust for, and which to leave alone.
:::

## Why draw graphs?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 520 270" width="100%" style="font-family:'Source Sans 3',sans-serif;font-size:22px">
  <defs>
    <marker id="grAh1" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#14213d"/></marker>
    <marker id="grAh1g" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#2e8b57"/></marker>
  </defs>
  <g fill="#eef1f7" stroke="#14213d" stroke-width="2.2">
    <ellipse cx="260" cy="42" rx="98" ry="30"/>
    <ellipse cx="88" cy="218" rx="84" ry="30"/>
    <ellipse cx="432" cy="218" rx="84" ry="30"/>
  </g>
  <g stroke-width="2.4" fill="none">
    <line x1="205" y1="66" x2="122" y2="186" stroke="#14213d" marker-end="url(#grAh1)"/>
    <line x1="315" y1="66" x2="398" y2="186" stroke="#14213d" marker-end="url(#grAh1)"/>
    <line x1="174" y1="218" x2="344" y2="218" stroke="#2e8b57" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#grAh1g)"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="#14213d" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="central">
    <text x="260" y="42">Stone size <tspan font-style="italic">X</tspan></text>
    <text x="88" y="218">Treatment <tspan font-style="italic">T</tspan></text>
    <text x="432" y="218">Success <tspan font-style="italic">Y</tspan></text>
  </g>
  <g fill="#5b6478" font-size="17px" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="118" y="112">doctors choose</text>
    <text x="408" y="112">harder to treat</text>
    <text x="260" y="252" fill="#2e8b57">the effect we want</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
Potential outcomes say what an effect **is**. A graph says **where the data came from** — and that decides what to adjust for.

- An arrow $X \to T$ means "$X$ is a direct cause of $T$": change $X$ and $T$ can change.
- This is a **DAG** — a *directed acyclic graph*: arrows have a direction, and you can never follow them back to where you started.
:::
::::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="The missing arrows are the strong claims"}
No arrow means "no direct effect". Here: no other common cause of treatment and success (for example, no unrecorded frailty that doctors acted on). If that is false, the graph — and every conclusion drawn from it — is false.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the kidney-stone graph aloud: doctors look at the stone size X before choosing; large stones are harder to treat whatever you do; and the green arrow is the effect we are after. Stress that drawing an arrow is a weak claim (it only says an effect *might* exist), while leaving one out is a strong claim. Likely question: "Where does the graph come from?" Answer: from subject-matter knowledge — clinicians, the study design, timing — not from the data alone.
:::

## Structural causal models: the equations behind the arrows

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block data-title="Definition 6 (Structural causal model)"}
An SCM has three ingredients:

1. the variables we model (here $X$, $T$, $Y$);
2. background factors $U$ with a distribution $P(U)$: everything we leave out of the model;
3. one assignment per modeled variable, ${v_i := f_i(\mathrm{pa}_i, u_i)}$, where $\mathrm{pa}_i$ are the **parents** (direct causes) of $v_i$.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block .example data-title="Running example: kidney stones"}
| ${X := f_X(U_X)}$ · stone size, set by nature
| ${T := f_T(X, U_T)}$ · the doctor's choice
| ${Y := f_Y(T, X, U_Y)}$ · success

Joint distribution, read off the graph:
${P(x, t, y) = P(x)\,P(t \mid x)\,P(y \mid t, x)}$
:::
:::
::::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Each line is a **mechanism**: read ":=" as "is produced by", not as an equation to rearrange; its arguments are the arrows into $v_i$. With independent background factors, the joint distribution **factorizes along the graph**: one factor per variable, given its parents.
:::

::: {.notes}
An SCM is just the graph with the mechanisms filled in. We almost never know the functions f — and we will not need them for effects at the population level — but thinking in mechanisms makes interventions easy to define, which is the next slide. The factorization is the bridge to data: each factor is something we can estimate. (In the literature the modeled variables are called endogenous and the background factors exogenous, and the factorization is the causal Markov condition — names only, nothing new.) Likely question: "Why can't I rearrange the equation?" Because Y := f(T, X) says Y listens to T; it does not say T listens to Y.
:::

## Interventions are graph surgery

