```{=html}
    <text x="890" y="68">X</text><text x="740" y="170">t</text><text x="1040" y="170">Y</text>
  </g>
  <text x="800" y="104" fill="#d1495b" font-size="26px" text-anchor="middle">✂</text>
  <g fill="#c8742b" font-size="18px" font-style="italic" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="120" y="228">T := f<tspan font-size="13px" dy="4">T</tspan><tspan dy="-4">(X, U</tspan><tspan font-size="13px" dy="4">T</tspan><tspan dy="-4">)</tspan></text>
    <text x="740" y="228">T := t</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

- $\operatorname{do}(T = t)$ **replaces T's mechanism** with the constant $t$ and leaves every other mechanism untouched.
- In the graph: **delete every arrow into $T$.** Nothing can influence $T$ any more — you set it.
- In the factorization: **drop $T$'s factor.** $P(x, y \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = P(x)\,P(y \mid t, x)$ — the *truncated factorization*.

::: {.notes}
This is Pearl's key move: an intervention is a local change to the model. The stone still has whatever size it has, and size still affects success; only the doctor's decision rule is overruled. Summing the truncated factorization over x gives the formula on the next slide. Connect to experiments: a randomized trial is exactly this — the coin, not the stone size, decides the treatment, so the arrow from X into T disappears.
:::

## Seeing versus doing, in one formula

$$
\underbrace{P(y \mid t) = \sum_x P(y \mid t, x)\,\color{#d1495b}{P(x \mid t)}}_{\text{seeing}}
\qquad\qquad
\underbrace{P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = \sum_x P(y \mid t, x)\,\color{#2e8b57}{P(x)}}_{\text{doing}}
$$

**Seeing** is the law of total probability over $X$, weighted by $P(x \mid t)$. **Doing** sums the truncated factorization over $x$: the intervention leaves $P(x)$ unchanged.

::: {.compact}
| Success rate of A ($T = 1$) | weight on small | weight on large | result |
|:------------------|:---------------:|:---------------:|:------:|
| Seeing: $P(Y=1 \mid T=1)$ | $P(\text{small} \mid T{=}1) = 0.25$ | $P(\text{large} \mid T{=}1) = 0.75$ | 78.0 % |
| Doing: $P(Y=1 \mid \operatorname{do}(T=1))$ | $P(\text{small}) = 0.51$ | $P(\text{large}) = 0.49$ | **83.3 %** |
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Both rows use A's within-size success rates (93.1 %, 73.0 %); only the **weights** differ. Seeing weights by *who happened to get* A; doing, by *the whole population*. For B ($T = 0$), doing gives 77.9 %: **+5.4 pp for A**, the standardization from Foundations.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to slow down on. The within-stratum success rates are identical in both formulas; the entire gap between "seeing" and "doing" is the case mix. A was handed 75 % large stones; under do(T = 1) everyone would get A, so the case mix is the population's 49 % large. Arithmetic for the curious: 0.25 × 93.1 + 0.75 × 73.0 = 78.0; 0.51 × 93.1 + 0.49 × 73.0 = 83.3. The "doing" formula comes from the previous slide's truncated factorization: just sum P(x) P(y | t, x) over x.
:::

## Three building blocks: chain, fork, collider

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1200 140" width="100%" height="125" style="font-family:'Source Sans 3',sans-serif;font-size:26px">
  <defs><marker id="grAh3" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#14213d"/></marker></defs>
  <g stroke="#c4cee0" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 5"><line x1="400" y1="10" x2="400" y2="130"/><line x1="800" y1="10" x2="800" y2="130"/></g>
  <g fill="none" stroke="#14213d" stroke-width="2.2">
    <circle cx="80" cy="50" r="27"/><circle cx="200" cy="50" r="27"/><circle cx="320" cy="50" r="27"/>
    <line x1="107" y1="50" x2="171" y2="50" marker-end="url(#grAh3)"/><line x1="227" y1="50" x2="291" y2="50" marker-end="url(#grAh3)"/>
    <circle cx="480" cy="50" r="27"/><circle cx="600" cy="50" r="27"/><circle cx="720" cy="50" r="27"/>
    <line x1="573" y1="50" x2="509" y2="50" marker-end="url(#grAh3)"/><line x1="627" y1="50" x2="691" y2="50" marker-end="url(#grAh3)"/>
    <circle cx="880" cy="50" r="27"/><circle cx="1000" cy="50" r="27"/><circle cx="1120" cy="50" r="27"/>
    <line x1="907" y1="50" x2="971" y2="50" marker-end="url(#grAh3)"/><line x1="1093" y1="50" x2="1029" y2="50" marker-end="url(#grAh3)"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="#14213d" font-style="italic" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="central">
    <text x="80" y="50">T</text><text x="200" y="50">M</text><text x="320" y="50">Y</text>
    <text x="480" y="50">T</text><text x="600" y="50">X</text><text x="720" y="50">Y</text>
    <text x="880" y="50">T</text><text x="1000" y="50">C</text><text x="1120" y="50">Y</text>
  </g>
  <g fill="#c8742b" font-weight="600" font-size="24px" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="200" y="115">Chain</text><text x="600" y="115">Fork</text><text x="1000" y="115">Collider</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

::: {.compact}
|  | Chain $T \to M \to Y$ | Fork $T \leftarrow X \to Y$ | Collider $T \to C \leftarrow Y$ |
|:--------------|:-------------------:|:-------------------------:|:-------------------:|
| In causal terms | $M$ is a **mediator**: it carries $T$'s effect | $X$ is a **confounder**: it causes both | $C$ is a **collider**: both cause it |
| Everyday example | smoking → tar → cancer | ice-cream sales ← hot weather → drownings | talent → fame ← looks |
| Are $T$ and $Y$ associated? | yes — causally | yes — but not causally | **no** |
| … after conditioning on the middle variable? | no — path **blocked** | no — path **blocked** | **yes — path opened** |
:::

[Every path in every DAG is built from these three pieces. The first two behave the way intuition expects; the collider is the one that surprises people.]{.small}

::: {.notes}
Conditioning means holding the middle variable fixed: stratifying on it, adjusting for it in a regression, or selecting only certain values of it. Chain: once you know the tar level, smoking tells you nothing more about cancer — and that is bad news if you wanted smoking's effect, because the effect runs through tar. Fork: on days with the same weather, ice-cream sales tell you nothing about drownings — conditioning on a confounder removes the spurious association, which is exactly what we want. Collider: talent and looks are unrelated in the population, but once you know someone is famous, learning they have little talent tells you they must be very good-looking. Next slide makes the collider concrete.
:::

## Collider bias: selection creates association {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{ojs}
viewof grBerkSel = Inputs.toggle({label: "Look only at the famous", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
grBerk = {
  const rng = mulberry32(11), rows = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 900; i++) {
    const talent = randn(rng), looks = randn(rng);
    rows.push({talent, looks, famous: talent + looks > 1.5});
  }
  return rows;
}
grCorr = rows => {
  const n = rows.length, mt = d3.mean(rows, d => d.talent), ml = d3.mean(rows, d => d.looks);
  let stl = 0, stt = 0, sll = 0;
  for (const d of rows) { stl += (d.talent - mt) * (d.looks - ml); stt += (d.talent - mt) ** 2; sll += (d.looks - ml) ** 2; }
  return stl / Math.sqrt(stt * sll);
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 540, height: 360, grid: true,
  marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [-3.5, 3.5], label: "Talent", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36},
  y: {domain: [-3.5, 3.5], label: "Looks"},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(grBerk.filter(d => !d.famous), {x: "talent", y: "looks", r: 2.3, fill: grBerkSel ? "#c3c9d6" : "#14213d", fillOpacity: grBerkSel ? 0.35 : 0.45}),
    Plot.dot(grBerk.filter(d => d.famous), {x: "talent", y: "looks", r: 3, fill: "#c8742b", fillOpacity: 0.85}),
    Plot.linearRegressionY(grBerkSel ? grBerk.filter(d => d.famous) : grBerk, {x: "talent", y: "looks", stroke: grBerkSel ? "#c8742b" : "#14213d", strokeWidth: 3, ci: 0})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
Talent and looks are **independent** here. An actor becomes famous (orange) when talent + looks is high enough.

Among the famous, a less talented actor **must** be unusually good-looking to have made it — so the two traits become **negatively** associated. Fame is a collider: Talent → Fame ← Looks.

```{ojs}
html`<div class="readout">
  corr(talent, looks), everyone: <b>${grCorr(grBerk).toFixed(2)}</b><br>
  corr(talent, looks), famous only: <b>${grCorr(grBerk.filter(d => d.famous)).toFixed(2)}</b>
</div>`
```

::: {.block .alert data-title="Why causal inference cares"}
Analyzing only survivors, only hospitalized patients, or only people who answered a follow-up survey **conditions on a collider** whenever treatment and outcome both affect who ends up in the sample. This is *Berkson's paradox*.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Flip the toggle. The navy regression line through everyone is flat; the orange line through the famous slopes down. Nothing causal connects talent and looks — the association is manufactured by selection. Berkson (1946) noticed the same thing in hospital data: two unrelated diseases both send people to hospital, so among inpatients they look negatively related. The lesson for causal inference: filtering or conditioning on a common effect of T and Y biases the estimate, and it can happen silently, through how the sample was collected.
:::

## d-separation: reading independence off the graph

A path between two variables (say $T$ and $Y$) is **blocked** by a set of variables $X$ if it contains

- a chain $\to V \to$ or a fork $\leftarrow V \to$ whose middle variable $V$ **is in** $X$, or
- a collider $\to V \leftarrow$ such that **neither $V$ nor any descendant of $V$** is in $X$ (a *descendant* of $V$ is anything $V$ causes, directly or indirectly).

$T$ and $Y$ are **d-separated** by $X$ if *every* path between them is blocked.

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 7 (d-separation implies independence)"}
If $T$ and $Y$ are d-separated by $X$ in $G$, then $T \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid X$ in every distribution compatible with $G$.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Paths are pipes that carry association. Chains and forks are **open until you condition on the middle**; colliders are **closed until you condition on them** (or on a descendant). All pipes closed: no association flows.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the only formal rule in the section, and it is just the three building blocks applied to every path. The descendant clause matters: conditioning on something caused by a collider (say, "appeared on a magazine cover", caused by fame) opens the collider too. Why care: d-separation turns a picture into a list of independences you can test, and it is the engine behind the backdoor criterion coming up. Students do not need to run it by hand on big graphs — software does that (code slide later).
:::

## d-separation, live {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{ojs}
viewof estructura = Inputs.radio(["Chain T → M → Y", "Fork T ← X → Y", "Collider T → C ← Y"], {value: "Chain T → M → Y"})
viewof condB = Inputs.toggle({label: "Condition on the middle variable", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
dsep = {
  const rng = mulberry32(5), n = 1200, rows = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    let T, mid, Y;
    if (estructura.startsWith("Chain")) { T = randn(rng); mid = T + randn(rng); Y = mid + randn(rng); }
    else if (estructura.startsWith("Fork")) { mid = randn(rng); T = mid + randn(rng); Y = mid + randn(rng); }
    else { T = randn(rng); Y = randn(rng); mid = T + Y + 0.5 * randn(rng); }
    rows.push({T, mid, Y});
  }
  const sd = Math.sqrt(rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r.mid * r.mid, 0) / n);
  rows.forEach(r => r.sel = Math.abs(r.mid) < 0.2 * sd);
  return rows;
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 330, grid: true,
  marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [-4.5, 4.5], label: "T", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36}, y: {domain: [-5, 5], label: "Y"},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(dsep, {x: "T", y: "Y", r: 2, fill: condB ? "#b9c1d0" : "#14213d", fillOpacity: condB ? 0.4 : 0.5}),
    condB ? Plot.dot(dsep.filter(d => d.sel), {x: "T", y: "Y", r: 3, fill: "#c8742b"}) : null,
    Plot.linearRegressionY(condB ? dsep.filter(d => d.sel) : dsep, {x: "T", y: "Y", stroke: condB ? "#c8742b" : "#14213d", strokeWidth: 3, ci: 0})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
```{ojs}
{
  const r = rows => {
    const n = rows.length, mt = d3.mean(rows, d => d.T), my = d3.mean(rows, d => d.Y);
    let sty = 0, stt = 0, syy = 0;
    for (const d of rows) { sty += (d.T - mt) * (d.Y - my); stt += (d.T - mt) ** 2; syy += (d.Y - my) ** 2; }
    return sty / Math.sqrt(stt * syy);
  };
  const all = r(dsep), sel = r(dsep.filter(d => d.sel));
  const kind = estructura.split(" ")[0], v = {Chain: "M", Fork: "X", Collider: "C"}[kind];
  const msg = {
    Chain: condB ? "Holding the mediator M fixed <b>blocks</b> the path: the correlation vanishes. Conditioning on a mediator hides a real effect."
                 : "T affects Y through M, so they are correlated — and this association is causal. Now condition on M.",
    Fork: condB ? "Holding the confounder X fixed <b>blocks</b> the back door: the spurious correlation vanishes."
                : "X drives both T and Y, so they are correlated even though T has no effect on Y. Now condition on X.",
    Collider: condB ? "Holding the collider C fixed <b>opens</b> the path: a strong correlation appears out of nothing."
                    : "T and Y both cause C but not each other: no correlation. Now condition on C."
  }[kind];
  return html`<div class="readout">
    corr(T, Y), all data: <b>${all.toFixed(2)}</b><br>
    corr(T, Y) among units with ${v} ≈ 0: <b>${condB ? sel.toFixed(2) : "tick the box"}</b><br><br>
    ${msg}
  </div>`;
}
```

[Orange points: units whose middle variable is close to 0 — holding it (nearly) fixed is what "conditioning" means.]{.small}

```r
library(dagitty)
g <- dagitty("dag { T -> C <- Y }")
dseparated(g, "T", "Y", list())   # TRUE: blocked at C
dseparated(g, "T", "Y", "C")      # FALSE: C opens it
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Suggested sequence: start on Chain — the cloud is tilted (T really affects Y through M); tick the box and the orange slice is flat, because holding M fixed blocks the effect. Switch to Fork: tilted again, but now the association is pure confounding; conditioning on X removes it, which is what we want. Finally Collider: a round cloud with no correlation; condition on C and the orange slice becomes a tilted band — the Berkson effect again. The orange slice approximates conditioning: we keep only units whose middle variable lies in a narrow band around zero. The dagitty lines give the collider verdicts from the graph alone, without any data.
:::

## The backdoor criterion

A **backdoor path** from $T$ to $Y$ is any path that starts with an arrow **into** $T$ ($T \leftarrow \cdots$). It carries association that is not causation.

::: {.block data-title="Definition 8 (Backdoor criterion)"}
A set $X$ of observed variables satisfies the backdoor criterion for $(T, Y)$ if
(i) no variable in $X$ is a descendant of $T$, and
(ii) $X$ blocks every backdoor path from $T$ to $Y$.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
**Close every back door into $T$, and never condition on anything $T$ causes.** Rule (ii) removes the non-causal association; rule (i) keeps mediators and downstream colliders out of the adjustment set.
:::

::: {.block .example data-title="Running example: kidney stones"}
The only backdoor path is $T \leftarrow X \to Y$. Conditioning on stone size $X$ blocks it (the middle of a fork), and the treatment does not change stone size. So $\{X\}$ works.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Backdoor" is a vivid name: association can leave T by its front door (arrows out of T, the causal effect) or sneak in by a back door (arrows into T, confounding). The criterion is a checklist you can run by eye on small graphs. Common confusion: condition (i) is not redundant with (ii) — a mediator does not lie on any backdoor path, so (ii) alone would not forbid it; (i) does.
:::

## The backdoor adjustment formula

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 9 (Backdoor adjustment)"}
If $X$ satisfies the backdoor criterion for $(T, Y)$, then
$$P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = \sum_x P(y \mid t, x)\, P(x).$$
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
**Compare treated and untreated within each level of $X$, then average over the whole population's $X$.** Everything on the right is observable: the causal question has become a statistical one.
:::

- Kidney stones, $X$ = stone size: this is the standardization we did by hand, **+5.4 pp** for A.
- It guarantees conditional ignorability, $(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid X$, and justifies regression, IPW and matching.

::: {.notes}
Callback to the opening hospital example: "were they already sicker?" is exactly the back door T ← severity → Y, and this formula is how you close it. For continuous X the sum becomes an integral. Point out that we have now derived the same formula three ways: by intuition (compare like with like), from potential outcomes (the identification theorem), and from the graph (truncated factorization plus the backdoor criterion). That convergence is the reassurance that these frameworks agree. The practical payoff: ignorability was an assumption stated in the abstract; the backdoor criterion lets you argue for it with an explicit story that colleagues can criticize arrow by arrow. Regression, IPW and matching are the estimators of Section 4.
:::

## Good controls and bad controls

::: {.compact}
| Role of the variable | Graph | Adjust? | Why |
|:-----------------------|:--------------------------|:------:|:------------------------------------|
| **Confounder** $X$ | $T \leftarrow X \to Y$ | ✓ yes | closes an open back door |
| **Mediator** $M$ | $T \to M \to Y$ | ✗ no | blocks part of the effect you want (overadjustment) |
| **Collider** $C$ | $T \to C \leftarrow Y$ | ✗ no | opens a spurious path (collider bias) |
| **Pre-treatment collider** $C$ | $T \leftarrow U_1 \to C \leftarrow U_2 \to Y$ | ✗ no | *M-bias* (from the M shape): opens a path via $U_1$ and $U_2$ |
| **Cause of $T$ only** $Z$ | $Z \to T \to Y$ | no need | adds variance; can amplify unmeasured confounding |
:::

- **Mediator:** for a stroke drug that lowers blood pressure, comparing patients with equal *post-treatment* pressure hides that part of its effect.
- **Collider:** analyzing only patients who came back for follow-up, when treatment and recovery both affect who comes back.

::: {.block .alert data-title="A tempting rule that is wrong"}
"Adjust for everything measured before treatment" fails under M-bias. **The graph decides**, not the timing (Cinelli, Forney & Pearl, 2022).
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the rows with the backdoor criterion in hand. Confounder: the classic good control — it sits on a back door. Mediator and collider: both are descendants of T, so rule (i) already forbids them. Pre-treatment collider: C is a collider of two unmeasured causes; the path T ← U1 → C ← U2 → Y is blocked as long as you leave C alone, and adjusting for C opens it. "M-bias" refers to the shape of the drawn graph, not to the mediator M. In practice M-bias is often small, and if C is also a confounder there is a genuine trade-off. Cause of T only (like the doctor on call): no back door runs through it, so it is not needed; adjusting for it removes useful variation in T and, if any unmeasured confounding remains, amplifies that bias.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
You want the **total effect** of a new drug $T$ on recovery $Y$ — its effect through all paths, including the one via $M$. For each variable: must you adjust for it, must you *not*, or is it optional?

```{ojs}
grOpts = ["Must adjust", "Must not adjust", "Optional"]
viewof grQX = Inputs.radio(grOpts, {label: "X · severity", value: null})
viewof grQM = Inputs.radio(grOpts, {label: "M · blood pressure", value: null})
viewof grQC = Inputs.radio(grOpts, {label: "C · came back", value: null})
viewof grQW = Inputs.radio(grOpts, {label: "W · gene", value: null})
viewof grQZ = Inputs.radio(grOpts, {label: "Z · doctor on call", value: null})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const items = [
    ["X", grQX, "Must adjust", "a confounder: T ← X → Y is an open back door."],
    ["M", grQM, "Must not adjust", "a mediator (a descendant of T): conditioning blocks part of the effect."],
    ["C", grQC, "Must not adjust", "a collider: T → C ← Y. Even analyzing only those who came back opens a spurious path."],
    ["W", grQW, "Optional", "affects only Y, so no back door runs through it. Adjusting is unbiased and usually sharpens the estimate."],
    ["Z", grQZ, "Optional", "affects only T, so it is not needed. Better left out: it adds variance and can amplify bias from unmeasured confounders."]
  ];
  const done = items.filter(d => d[1] != null);
  if (!done.length) return html`<div class="readout quiz">Make a call for each variable to see feedback.</div>`;
  const ok = done.filter(d => d[1] === d[2]).length;
  return html`<div class="readout quiz ${ok === done.length ? "good" : "bad"}">
    ${done.map(d => `<div>${d[1] === d[2] ? `✓ <b>${d[0]}: ${d[2].toLowerCase()}</b>` : `✗ <b>${d[0]}: the answer is “${d[2].toLowerCase()}”</b>`} — ${d[3]}</div>`).join("")}
    <div style="margin-top:4px"><b>${ok} of ${done.length}</b> correct${done.length < 5 ? " so far" : ""}.</div>
  </div>`;
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Give students a minute before anyone clicks. Answers: X must be adjusted (confounder); M and C must not (mediator, collider — both are descendants of T, so the backdoor criterion's rule (i) already rules them out); W and Z are optional, but for opposite reasons in practice. W explains outcome variation, so adjusting for it typically shrinks the standard error. Z only moves T; adjusting for it throws away useful variation in treatment, inflating the variance, and if there is any unmeasured confounding it amplifies that bias. Z behaves like an instrument — it comes back in the designs section.
:::
