```{=html}
    <text x="380" y="36">Genotype <tspan font-style="italic">U</tspan> (unobserved)</text>
    <text x="100" y="160">Smoking <tspan font-style="italic">T</tspan></text>
    <text x="380" y="160">Tar <tspan font-style="italic">M</tspan></text>
    <text x="660" y="160">Cancer <tspan font-style="italic">Y</tspan></text>
  </g>
  <text x="380" y="205" fill="#c8742b" font-size="17px" text-anchor="middle">orange: step 2's back door M ← T ← U → Y, closed by adjusting for T</text>
</svg>
```

An unmeasured gene $U$ might drive smoking and cancer, so no backdoor adjustment works. But if smoking affects cancer **only through tar**, chain two identifiable effects:

1. **Smoking → tar.** The only back door, $T \leftarrow U \to Y \leftarrow M$, is blocked at the collider $Y$, so seeing = doing: ${P(m \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = P(m \mid t)}$.
2. **Tar → cancer.** Adjusting for $T$ blocks the back door $M \leftarrow T \leftarrow U \to Y$: ${P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(m)) = \sum_{t'} P(y \mid m, t')\,P(t')}$.
3. **Chain them.** Because $T$ affects $Y$ only through $M$, ${P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = \sum_m P(m \mid \operatorname{do}(t))\,P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(m))}$; substitute steps 1 and 2.

::: {.notes}
Optional slide. This is Pearl's famous example, built on the tobacco industry's old argument that a gene, not smoking, causes cancer. The logic: we cannot see U, but U has to act on cancer through a different route than tar does. Step 1 needs no adjustment at all, because the only non-causal path from smoking to tar runs into cancer from both sides — a collider. Step 2 is an ordinary backdoor adjustment with T as the adjustment set: the orange path in the picture is the back door it closes. Step 3 composes the two: the effect of smoking on cancer is the effect of tar on cancer, averaged over the tar levels that smoking produces. (Formally, step 3 itself uses the frontdoor conditions on the next slide, via rules 2 and 3 of do-calculus.)
:::

## The frontdoor formula {.deeper}

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Frontdoor adjustment"}
If (i) $M$ intercepts every directed path from $T$ to $Y$, (ii) there is no unblocked backdoor path from $T$ to $M$, and (iii) $T$ blocks every backdoor path from $M$ to $Y$, then
$$P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = \sum_m \underbrace{P(m \mid t)}_{\text{step 1: } T \to M} \; \underbrace{\sum_{t'} P(y \mid m, t')\, P(t')}_{\text{step 2: } M \to Y}.$$
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
**Average the effect of tar on cancer over the tar levels that smoking would produce.** An unobserved confounder does not automatically doom identification: a fully observed mechanism can route around it.
:::

[**Honest caveat:** these conditions are strong, and doubtful for real smoking data. Frontdoor designs are rare in practice; the idea matters more than the formula.]{.small}

::: {.notes}
Optional slide. Read the formula from the inside out: the inner sum is the effect of setting tar to m (step 2, a backdoor adjustment for T); the outer sum weights it by how likely each tar level is when we set smoking to t (step 1). The 3D graph on the next slide satisfies these conditions too: there, X is observed and U is not, and M carries the whole effect of T. That is why the 3D status box says the frontdoor path via M identifies the effect even though no backdoor adjustment does.
:::

## Graph surgery in 3D {data-menu-title="DAG 3D"}

::: {.three-stage data-three="dag" data-prevent-swipe="" style="height: 450px"}
:::

[Two back doors ($T \leftarrow X \to Y$ and $T \leftarrow U \to Y$) and one causal path through the mediator $M$. **Adjust for X** closes one back door; $U$ is unmeasured, so the other stays open. **do(T)** deletes both. **Adjust for M** would block the effect itself. Clicking a node does the same as its button.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
Drive this live; it pulls the whole section together. Start with everything open: two orange back doors and the green causal path through M. Click "Adjust for X": the X back door goes gray, but the U back door stays orange — you cannot adjust for what you did not measure, so no backdoor set exists here. Reset and click "do(T)": both back doors vanish because nothing points into T any more; this is why experiments are the gold standard. Then "Adjust for M": the green path is blocked — overadjustment. With everything open, the status box notes that the frontdoor route via M still identifies the effect. Clicking T, X or M toggles the same switches as the buttons. The next slide asks software to confirm all of this.
:::

## In code: identification from the DAG

Software does the path-checking for you. Here is the graph from the 3D scene: observed $X$ and latent $U$ confound $T$ and $Y$; $M$ mediates.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R · dagitty

```r
library(dagitty)
g <- dagitty("dag {
  X -> T ; X -> Y
  U -> T ; U -> Y
  T -> M -> Y
  U [latent]
}")
adjustmentSets(g, exposure = "T", outcome = "Y")  # prints nothing: no valid set, latent U keeps T <- U -> Y open
adjustmentSets(g, exposure = "M", outcome = "Y")  # { T }: step 2 of the frontdoor
impliedConditionalIndependencies(g)               # testable implication: M _||_ X | T
```

### Python · DoWhy

```python
from dowhy import CausalModel

model = CausalModel(
    data=df, treatment="T", outcome="Y",
    graph="digraph { X -> T; X -> Y; U -> T; U -> Y; T -> M; M -> Y; }",
)  # U is not a column of df, so DoWhy treats it as unobserved
estimand = model.identify_effect()        # no backdoor set; finds the frontdoor estimand via M
print(estimand)
est = model.estimate_effect(estimand, method_name="frontdoor.two_stage_regression")
```
:::

[`impliedConditionalIndependencies` lists what the graph predicts you should see in the data — a cheap way to catch a wrong graph.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
The dagitty output reproduces what we argued by hand: no backdoor set exists for T on Y because U is latent; for M on Y the set {T} works, which is step 2 of the frontdoor. The implied independence M ⫫ X | T is a falsifiable prediction: if it fails clearly in your data, an arrow is missing (for instance X → M). Passing such tests does not prove the graph right, but failing them proves it wrong.
:::

## do-calculus {.smaller .deeper}

Backdoor and frontdoor are special cases. The general engine is three rules. **Notation change:** on this slide $X, Y, Z, W$ are *generic*, disjoint sets of variables, and $X$ is the set we intervene on (not the covariates of earlier slides). $G_{\overline{X}}$ deletes arrows *into* $X$; $G_{\underline{Z}}$ deletes arrows *out of* $Z$.

1. **Ignore an observation:** $P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), z, w) = P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), w)$ if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)$ in $G_{\overline{X}}$.<br>[After intervening on $X$, observing $Z$ adds no information about $Y$.]{.muted}
2. **Swap an action for an observation:** $P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), \operatorname{do}(z), w) = P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), z, w)$ if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)$ in $G_{\overline{X}\underline{Z}}$.<br>[Setting $Z$ equals seeing $Z$ when no back door from $Z$ to $Y$ is open.]{.muted}
3. **Ignore an action:** $P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), \operatorname{do}(z), w) = P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), w)$ if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)$ in $G_{\overline{X}\,\overline{Z(W)}}$, where $Z(W)$ are the $Z$-nodes that are not ancestors of any $W$-node in $G_{\overline{X}}$.<br>[Intervening on $Z$ is irrelevant when it cannot reach $Y$.]{.muted}

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 10 (Completeness: Shpitser–Pearl; Huang–Valtorta, 2006)"}
A causal effect is identifiable from $P(v)$ and $G$ **if and only if** it can be rewritten without any $\operatorname{do}(\cdot)$ using these three rules.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
The goal is to transform an expression with $\operatorname{do}$ into one with only ordinary conditional probabilities. If the rules cannot do it, **no method can** without extra assumptions. Software (dagitty, DoWhy, the ID algorithm) applies them for you.
:::

::: {.notes}
Optional slide: skip it on a first pass. Each rule says when you may delete or convert a term, and each condition is a d-separation check in a modified graph. The completeness result is what makes do-calculus powerful: it is not one trick among many, it is the full answer to "can this effect be identified from observational data and this graph?" Remind students of the change of letters: here X is whatever we intervene on, not the covariates.
:::

## Counterfactuals in an SCM {.smaller .deeper}

Rung 3 of the ladder: "*this* patient took B and failed — would A have worked for *her*?" With a full SCM, answer in three steps:

1. **Abduction** — use what you saw about this unit to update the background factors: $P(U) \to P(U \mid \text{evidence})$.
2. **Action** — modify the model with $\operatorname{do}(T = t)$.
3. **Prediction** — compute $Y$ in the modified model, using the updated $U$.

::: {.block .example data-title="A tiny worked example"}
Model: $Y := T + U$. We observed $T = 0,\ Y = 1$. **Abduction:** $U = Y - T = 1$. **Action:** set $T = 1$. **Prediction:** $Y = 1 + 1 = 2$. Had this unit been treated, its outcome would have been 2.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="Why rung 3 needs more than rung 2"}
Interventional questions average over $P(U)$; counterfactuals need *this unit's* $U$, so they depend on the exact form of $f$. Two models can agree on every ${P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t))}$ yet disagree on counterfactuals. With $U \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.5)$, both $Y := U$ and $Y := T \oplus U$ (exclusive or) give ${P(Y = 1 \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = 0.5}$ for every $t$. But after seeing $T = 0,\ Y = 1$, the first model says $Y(1) = 1$ and the second says $Y(1) = 0$.
:::

[So counterfactuals are identified only with extra assumptions (e.g. monotonicity); otherwise quantities such as the probabilities of necessity and sufficiency can be bounded.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
Optional slide. The worked example makes the three steps mechanical. The XOR example is the real lesson: data from experiments pin down rung 2, but rung 3 asks about individuals, and two mechanisms that look identical in every experiment can give opposite individual answers. This is why most applied work — and the rest of this deck — targets average effects (rung 2), which data plus assumptions can actually identify.
:::

## Recap: Causal graphs {.recap}

- A **DAG** writes down your causal story. Arrows allow effects; **missing arrows are the strong assumptions**.
- An intervention $\operatorname{do}(T = t)$ is **graph surgery**: delete the arrows into $T$. Seeing weights strata by $P(x \mid t)$; doing weights them by $P(x)$.
- **Chains and forks** carry association until you condition on the middle; **colliders** block it until you condition on them.
- **Backdoor criterion:** block every back door into $T$, condition on nothing $T$ causes. Kidney stones: $\{X\}$ works, giving +5.4 pp.
- **One formula, many names:** standardization = identification formula = backdoor adjustment = g‑formula. g‑computation and IPW (Section 4) are two ways to *estimate* it.

[**Test yourself:** name a pre-treatment variable you must *not* adjust for.]{.small}

::: {.notes}
Ask students to state the backdoor criterion in one sentence without notation before moving on — "close every back door, don't touch anything T causes" is the target. Test-yourself answer: a pre-treatment collider of two unobserved causes, as in M-bias (T ← U1 → C ← U2 → Y): adjusting for C opens a path that was blocked. (A cause of T only, like the doctor on call, is better left out too, but adjusting for it adds no bias unless there is unmeasured confounding.) Then bridge: identification gave us a formula in terms of observable probabilities, and even with unobserved confounders other routes (frontdoor, do-calculus) sometimes deliver one. The next section is about estimating that formula well when X has many values or is continuous, where we cannot just make a table.
:::

# Classical Estimation {#classical-estimation .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Many tools, one goal: recover a comparison that nature did not hand us.]{.section-subtitle}

```{=html}
<div class="pipeline"><div><b>1 · Question</b></div><div><b>2 · Estimand</b></div><div><b>3 · Identification</b></div><div class="on"><b>4 · Estimation</b></div><div class="on"><b>5 · Uncertainty</b></div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
We now know *what* we want (the estimand) and *when* the data can deliver it (identification: ignorability, positivity, or a valid backdoor set). This section is about turning the identification formula into an actual number from a finite sample, and then saying how sure we are. Throughout, we assume all confounders are measured — the next section drops that assumption.
:::

## From a formula to a number: three strategies {.smaller}

Identification gave us a formula built only from things we can observe:
$$\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}_X\big[\mu_1(X) - \mu_0(X)\big], \qquad \mu_t(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = t, X = x].$$
Estimation turns it into a number. There are three families of estimators:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.block data-title="1 · Model the outcome"}
Learn how $Y$ depends on $T$ and $X$: the regression $\mu_t(x)$.

→ regression, g-computation
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.block data-title="2 · Model the treatment"}
Learn who gets treated: the propensity score $e(x)$.

→ inverse probability weighting, matching
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.block data-title="3 · Model both"}
Use each model to correct the other's mistakes.

→ doubly robust (AIPW), double machine learning
:::
:::
::::

::: {.block .example data-title="Running example: kidney stones"}
With one binary covariate (stone size) every model can be fitted exactly, cell by cell, so all three families give the same answer: **+5.4 pp** in favor of A. With many or continuous covariates, models must smooth and extrapolate — and they can be wrong in different ways. That is when the choice matters.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide is the map for the whole section. The formula on top is the identification result from the potential-outcomes section: average, over the population's covariates, the difference between the expected outcome of treated and untreated units with those covariates. Strategy 1 estimates the inner regression functions mu_t. Strategy 2 never models the outcome; it models the treatment assignment and reweights. Strategy 3 does both. The kidney-stone numbers agree exactly because stone size is a single binary variable: there is nothing to extrapolate. Students should expect the methods to disagree on real data, and the disagreement is informative.
:::

## Regression adjustment

The most familiar tool: put the treatment and the confounders in one regression.
$$Y = \alpha + \tau T + X^\top \beta + \varepsilon$$

- $\hat\tau$ compares treated and untreated units **with the same $X$**, using the linear model to line them up.
- Kidney stones: success on $T$ plus a large-stone dummy gives $\hat\tau = 5.4$ pp.
- $Y$ is 0/1: OLS is then a *linear probability model* (differences in success rates).

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
"Holding $X$ fixed" is exactly what ignorability asks for. Regression does the holding-fixed with a formula instead of by splitting the data into strata.
:::

[$\hat\tau$ is the ATE only if the linear model is right **and** the effect is the same for everyone. More on that shortly.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
Students have run this regression many times; the new part is the causal reading. The coefficient on T is a causal effect only because we argued, with the DAG, that X closes every backdoor path, and only if the functional form is right. Why OLS with a 0/1 outcome is fine here: the linear probability model estimates differences in probabilities directly, and with T × X interactions (a saturated model, one parameter per cell) its fitted values reproduce the four cell success rates exactly — 93.1, 73.0, 86.7 and 68.75 percent. Keep the reading concrete: on the kidney stones, the regression of success on T and a large-stone dummy returns 5.38 pp. The small print at the bottom is a promise: shortly (after the optional FWL slide) we see what the coefficient means when the effect differs across groups.
:::

## Under the hood: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell {.deeper}

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 11 (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell)"}
The coefficient $\hat\tau$ from the full regression equals the slope from regressing $\tilde Y = Y - \hat Y(X)$ on $\tilde T = T - \hat T(X)$, where $\hat Y(X)$ and $\hat T(X)$ are the fitted values from regressing $Y$ and $T$ on $X$ alone.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Regression first strips out of $T$ and out of $Y$ everything that $X$ can predict ("partialling out"). What is left of $T$ is the part of treatment assignment that $X$ does not explain — the "as-if random" part — and $\hat\tau$ measures how the leftover $Y$ moves with it.
:::

If $X$ predicts $T$ almost perfectly, $\tilde T \approx 0$: nothing is left to learn from and $\hat\tau$ is very noisy — positivity failing, seen through regression.

```r
ry <- resid(lm(Y ~ X1 + X2, data = d))   # part of Y that X cannot predict
rt <- resid(lm(T ~ X1 + X2, data = d))   # part of T that X cannot predict
coef(lm(ry ~ rt))[2]                     # identical to ...
coef(lm(Y ~ T + X1 + X2, data = d))["T"] # ... the coefficient on T
```

::: {.notes}
FWL is worth knowing because it tells you where the regression gets its information: only from treatment variation that is not explained by the covariates. Two consequences. First, a precision warning: when the covariates nearly determine treatment, the residualized treatment has tiny variance and the standard error blows up. Second, "residualize both, then compare" is the seed of double/debiased machine learning later in this section, where the residualizing is done with flexible ML models instead of linear regressions. The code runs as is in base R; the two printed numbers agree to machine precision.
:::

## When the coefficient is not the ATE

If the effect differs across groups, $\tau(x) = \text{CATE}(x)$, the coefficient from $Y \sim T + X$ averages the $\tau(x)$ with **its own weights**:
$$\hat\tau \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{\sum_x \mathbb{P}(X = x)\; e(x)\,\big(1 - e(x)\big)\; \tau(x)}{\sum_x \mathbb{P}(X = x)\; e(x)\,\big(1 - e(x)\big)}$$

- Most weight where treatment is split near 50/50; almost none where nearly everyone (or no one) is treated.
- Kidney stones: weights 0.52 / 0.48 vs population 0.51 / 0.49, so $\hat\tau = 5.38$ vs ATE $5.37$ pp.
- Had 98 % of large-stone patients got A: weight 0.09 for large stones, $\hat\tau = 6.2$ pp — nearly the small-stone effect.

[**The fix:** let the effect vary ($T \times X$), predict for everyone, average — that is **g-computation**, next.]{.hl}

::: {.notes}
This is a classic result (Angrist, 1998), for a regression with a dummy for every covariate group. The regression with an additive treatment term and a full set of group dummies does not average the group effects with the population shares; it weights each group by how much treatment varies within it, e(x)(1 − e(x)), times the group's size. Intuition: the regression learns most where it has both treated and untreated units to compare. On the kidney stones the weights are 0.51 × 0.244 × 0.756 = 0.094 for small stones and 0.49 × 0.767 × 0.233 = 0.088 for large stones; normalized, 0.518 and 0.482, close to the population shares 0.51 and 0.49, so the answer barely moves (5.38 versus 5.37 pp). Thought experiment on the slide: if e(large) were 0.98, its raw weight would be 0.49 × 0.98 × 0.02 = 0.0096 against 0.094 for small stones, so normalized 0.09 versus 0.91, and the coefficient would be 0.91 × 6.44 + 0.09 × 4.25 = 6.2 pp — almost purely the small-stone effect, even though half the population has large stones. The fix is to stop asking one coefficient to summarize a heterogeneous effect: model the outcome flexibly and average the predictions, which is g-computation.
:::

## g-computation: fill in the missing column

Remember the [?]{.q} cells in the potential-outcomes table? g-computation fills them in with model predictions.

1. Fit an outcome model $\hat\mu_t(x)$ that lets the effect vary with $X$ (e.g. $T \times X$ interactions).
2. For **every** unit, predict both potential outcomes: $\hat Y_i(1) = \hat\mu_1(X_i)$ and $\hat Y_i(0) = \hat\mu_0(X_i)$.
3. Average the difference: $\hat\tau = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \big[\hat\mu_1(X_i) - \hat\mu_0(X_i)\big]$.

::: {.compact}
| Stone size | Patients | $\hat\mu_1$ (A) | $\hat\mu_0$ (B) | Difference |
|:-----------|:--------:|:---------------:|:---------------:|:----------:|
| Small | 357 | 93.1 % | 86.7 % | +6.4 pp |
| Large | 343 | 73.0 % | 68.8 % | +4.3 pp |
| **All 700 patients** | | **83.3 %** | **77.9 %** | **+5.4 pp** |
:::

```r
fit <- lm(Y ~ T * (X1 + X2), data = d)                 # the effect may vary with X
mean(predict(fit, newdata = transform(d, T = 1)) -     # everyone gets treatment ...
     predict(fit, newdata = transform(d, T = 0)))      # ... minus everyone gets control
```

::: {.notes}
The "g" stands for "generalized": Robins (1986) introduced the g-formula, which is the identification formula itself; g-computation just plugs a fitted model into it. Point out the conceptual move: we predict the outcome each patient would have had under A, and under B, even for patients we only saw under one of them. That is exactly filling in the question marks. The table shows it on the kidney stones: the model is just the four observed success rates, and averaging over all 700 patients (51 percent small, 49 percent large) gives 83.3 versus 77.9 percent. Unlike the single coefficient on the previous slides, this averages over the population's covariate distribution, so it targets the ATE even when the effect differs between strata. The price: it is only as good as the outcome model.
:::

## The propensity score

::: {.block data-title="Definition 12 (Propensity score)"}
$e(x) = \mathbb{P}(T = 1 \mid X = x)$: the probability that a unit with covariates $x$ receives the treatment.
:::

Kidney stones: $e(\text{small}) = 0.24$ but $e(\text{large}) = 0.77$ — large-stone patients were three times as likely to get A.

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 13 (Rosenbaum–Rubin, 1983)"}
If $(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid X$ and $0 < e(X) < 1$, then $(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid e(X)$.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Among units with the same propensity score, who got treated is as good as a coin flip that lands "treated" with probability $e(x)$ — a mini randomized experiment. So instead of matching on twenty covariates, we can use **one number**.
:::

[In practice $e(x)$ must be estimated (often by logistic regression), and it balances only the covariates you put into it.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
The kidney-stone numbers are 87/357 and 263/343. The propensity score is the second strategy's workhorse. The definition is just a conditional probability; the theorem is what makes it useful. Its real content: whatever adjustment works with the full covariate vector X also works with the scalar e(X). That reduction from many dimensions to one is why propensity scores became so popular for matching and weighting. Common student question: "Does the propensity score remove confounding by unmeasured variables?" No — it only balances what is in X. If doctors also used unrecorded frailty, the propensity score built from stone size cannot account for it.
:::

## Why one number is enough {.deeper .smaller}

::: {.block data-title="Proof of the Rosenbaum–Rubin theorem"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}\big(T=1 \mid Y(0), Y(1), e(X)\big) &= \mathbb{E}\big[\,\mathbb{E}(T \mid Y(0), Y(1), X) \;\big|\; Y(0), Y(1), e(X)\big] && \text{(1) tower property} \\
&= \mathbb{E}\big[\,e(X) \;\big|\; Y(0), Y(1), e(X)\big] && \text{(2) ignorability} \\
&= e(X). && \text{(3) we condition on } e(X)
\end{aligned}
$$
The probability of treatment does not depend on $(Y(0), Y(1))$ once we know $e(X)$, so $T \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1)) \mid e(X)$. $\square$
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="Reading the proof"}
- **Line 1** is allowed because $e(X)$ is a function of $X$: conditioning on $X$ carries at least as much information as conditioning on $e(X)$.
- **Line 2** is where the assumption enters: given $X$, treatment does not depend on the potential outcomes, so $\mathbb{E}(T \mid Y(0), Y(1), X) = \mathbb{P}(T = 1 \mid X) = e(X)$.
- The same argument shows the **balancing property** $X \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid e(X)$: replace $(Y(0), Y(1))$ by $X$.
:::

::: {.notes}
Optional slide. The proof is three lines and uses only the tower property of conditional expectation, which these students know. Walk through it once, pointing at which assumption each line uses. The balancing property in the last bullet is what you check in practice: after matching or weighting on the estimated score, covariate distributions should look the same in both groups.
:::

## IPW by hand: the kidney stones

Don't model the outcome — **reweight** patients so each treatment group looks like the whole population.

::: {.compact}
| Group | Patients | Chance of this treatment | Weight = 1 / chance | Weighted count |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A, small stones | 87 | 0.244 | 4.10 | 357 |
| A, large stones | 263 | 0.767 | 1.30 | 343 |
| B, small stones | 270 | 1 − 0.244 = 0.756 | 1.32 | 357 |
| B, large stones | 80 | 1 − 0.767 = 0.233 | 4.29 | 343 |
:::

- After weighting, **each** arm has 357 small-stone and 343 large-stone patients — the population's mix, as if a coin had assigned treatment.
- Weighted success rates: A **83.3 %**, B **77.9 %** → **+5.4 pp**, exactly the standardization answer.

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
Only 24 % of small-stone patients got A, so each one who did "stands in" for about four small-stone patients. Rare-for-their-type patients get big weights.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the most important slide for building intuition about weighting, so go slowly. Compute one row aloud: 87 small-stone patients got A, out of 357 small-stone patients, so e = 0.244 and each of them gets weight 4.10; 87 times 4.10 is 357. Do the same for B-large: only 80 of 343 large-stone patients got B, weight 4.29, and 80 times 4.29 is 343. Each arm becomes a "pseudo-population" of 700 with the population's 51/49 mix of stone sizes, so the comparison is no longer tilted by case mix. The weighted success rate for A is (81 × 4.10 + 192 × 1.30) / 700 = 83.3 percent; for B, (234 × 1.32 + 55 × 4.29) / 700 = 77.9 percent. Equality with standardization is exact here because the propensity score is estimated by cell frequencies.
:::

## Inverse probability weighting in general

$$
\hat\tau_{\text{IPW}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ \frac{T_i Y_i}{\hat e(X_i)} - \frac{(1-T_i) Y_i}{1 - \hat e(X_i)} \right]
$$

Read it as: reweighted treated mean minus reweighted control mean, where each unit is weighted by the **inverse probability** of the treatment it actually got.

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
A treated unit that had probability $e$ of being treated represents $1/e$ units like it. On average, the weights exactly undo the selective assignment.
:::

- Under ignorability and positivity, with the true $e$, IPW is **unbiased** for the ATE (proof on the next slide).
- We must divide by $e(X)$ and $1 - e(X)$: if either is 0 the formula breaks — that is positivity again.

::: {.notes}
The formula is the kidney-stone computation written for any covariates. Connect the formula to the table on the previous slide: the first sum is the weighted success rate in arm A, the second in arm B. The plain-words box is the key intuition. If e(X) is exactly 0 for some patients, no weight can make them count — that is a positivity failure. Two slides from now: what happens when e(X) is merely close to 0 or 1.
:::

## Why IPW is unbiased {.deeper}

::: {.block data-title="Claim: with the true propensity score, the weighted treated mean is unbiased for E[Y(1)]"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{T\,Y}{e(X)}\Big] &= \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{T\,Y(1)}{e(X)}\Big] && \text{consistency: if } T = 1 \text{ then } Y = Y(1) \\
&= \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\mathbb{E}\big(T \mid X, Y(1)\big)}{e(X)}\, Y(1)\Big] && \text{tower property: condition on } X, Y(1) \\
&= \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{e(X)}{e(X)}\, Y(1)\Big] = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)] && \text{ignorability: } \mathbb{E}(T \mid X, Y(1)) = e(X)
\end{aligned}
$$
The same argument with $1 - e(X)$ gives $\mathbb{E}\big[(1-T)\,Y/(1 - e(X))\big] = \mathbb{E}[Y(0)]$.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="Where each assumption is used"}
Consistency links the observed $Y$ to $Y(1)$; ignorability makes the chance of treatment cancel the weight; positivity ($e(X) > 0$) lets us divide at all.
:::

::: {.notes}
Optional slide. Every step uses something students already know. Line 1: for treated units the observed outcome is Y(1), and for untreated units T = 0 kills the term anyway. Line 2: condition on X and Y(1) inside the expectation; everything except T is then fixed. Line 3: ignorability says that, given X, treatment does not depend on Y(1), so the expected value of T is just e(X), which cancels the denominator. This is the whole reason the weights are "inverse probabilities". With an estimated e-hat the result holds approximately, provided the propensity model is right.
:::

## When weights explode {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- If some units have $\hat e(X)$ near 0 or 1, their weights $1/\hat e$ or $1/(1-\hat e)$ are **huge**: a few units dominate the estimate and its variance explodes. This is a *near*-violation of positivity.
- **Diagnose** with three numbers and one plot: the histogram of $\hat e$ in each group (do they overlap?), the largest weight, and the **effective sample size**
  $$\text{ESS} = \frac{\big(\sum_i w_i\big)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2},$$
  how many equally weighted units the weighted sample is worth.
- Kidney stones: largest weight 4.29, ESS 508 of 700 — mild.

[Simulation (same set-up as the lab later): $T \sim \text{Bernoulli}\big(\text{expit}(\gamma\,(0.7X_1 + 0.9X_2))\big)$, where $\text{expit}(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$ is the inverse logit; $\hat e$ is fitted by logistic regression, $n = 1000$.]{.small .muted}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{ojs}
viewof esGamma = Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 1.2, step: 0.1, label: "Confounding γ"})
```

```{ojs}
esOverlap = {
  const rng = mulberry32(7), n = 1000, rows = [], T = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const x1 = randn(rng), x2 = randn(rng);
    const t = rng() < expit(esGamma * (0.7 * x1 + 0.9 * x2)) ? 1 : 0;
    rows.push([1, x1, x2]); T.push(t);
  }
  const b = logitFit(rows, T);
  const units = rows.map((r, i) => {
    const e = expit(b[0] + b[1] * r[1] + b[2] * r[2]);
    return {e, t: T[i], w: T[i] ? 1 / e : 1 / (1 - e)};
  });
  const sw = d3.sum(units, d => d.w), sw2 = d3.sum(units, d => d.w * d.w);
  const bins = d3.range(20).map(k => ({lo: k / 20, hi: (k + 1) / 20, nt: 0, nc: 0}));
  for (const u of units) { const k = Math.min(19, Math.floor(u.e * 20)); if (u.t) bins[k].nt++; else bins[k].nc++; }
  return {bins, n, ess: sw * sw / sw2, wmax: d3.max(units, d => d.w),
          extreme: units.filter(d => d.e < 0.05 || d.e > 0.95).length};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 290, marginLeft: 56, marginBottom: 44,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Estimated propensity score ê(X)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36},
  y: {label: "units (treated ↑, control ↓)", tickFormat: Math.abs, grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(esOverlap.bins, {x1: "lo", x2: "hi", y: "nt", fill: "#c8742b", fillOpacity: 0.85, inset: 0.5}),
    Plot.rectY(esOverlap.bins, {x1: "lo", x2: "hi", y: d => -d.nc, fill: "#14213d", fillOpacity: 0.75, inset: 0.5}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const o = esOverlap, r = o.ess / o.n;
  return html`<div class="readout">Orange (up): treated · navy (down): control<br>
    Largest weight: <b>${o.wmax.toFixed(1)}</b> · ESS: <b>${o.ess.toFixed(0)}</b> of ${o.n} · units with ê &lt; 0.05 or &gt; 0.95: <b>${o.extreme}</b><br>
    ${r > 0.85 ? "Good overlap: every kind of unit appears in both groups, and the weights stay moderate."
      : r > 0.5 ? "Overlap is thinning: near ê = 0 and 1 one group is almost absent, so its few members there get big weights."
      : "Poor overlap: the tails hold almost only one group. IPW now leans on a handful of units — a near-violation of positivity."}</div>`;
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This slide shows the diagnostic every IPW analysis should start with: the overlap histogram. Orange bars above the axis are treated units, navy bars below are controls, binned by their estimated propensity score. At gamma = 0 both groups pile up around 0.5, the largest weight is about 2.4 and the ESS is essentially the full 1000. At the default gamma = 1.2 the groups spread toward opposite ends; the largest weight is about 39 and the ESS has dropped to about 540. At gamma = 3 the tails are almost one-coloured: about 360 units have e-hat below 0.05 or above 0.95, the largest weight exceeds 100, and the 1000 units are worth fewer than 150. ESS is defined on the slide: it is the sample size of an equally weighted sample that would have the same variance as the weighted mean. Expit is just the inverse of the logit, the function logistic regression uses to turn a linear score into a probability.
:::

## Seeing overlap: the propensity surface in 3D {data-menu-title="Propensity 3D"}

::: {.three-stage data-three="propensity" data-prevent-swipe="" style="height: 500px"}
:::

[Surface: $e(x)$ over two covariates; dots: units (orange treated, blue control). Slide **confounding γ** up from 0: the surface becomes a cliff, overlap vanishes, and with **Size = IPW weight** a few huge dots dominate.]{.small .muted}

::: {.notes}
Press "Size = IPW weight" first, so each dot is drawn in proportion to its weight. Drag gamma to 0: the surface is flat at 0.5, every unit has weight 2 and the effective sample size is the full 300. Back at the default gamma = 1 the surface is a gentle slope, yet a few units already carry large weights (the status box shows the maximum, around 20, and an effective sample size near half of 300). Now drag gamma toward 4: the surface turns into a step — on one side almost everyone is treated, on the other almost no one — and the handful of controls on the "treated" side get enormous weights. Ask the class: is IPW still unbiased in principle? Yes, if the propensity model is right — but it is so noisy that a single unit can swing the estimate. Drag to rotate the scene. Next: what to do about extreme weights.
:::

## Remedies: Hájek, trimming, ATT weights

- **Hájek (normalized) weights** — divide by the sum of the weights in each arm instead of by $n$:
  $$\hat\mu_1^{\text{Hájek}} = \frac{\sum_i T_i Y_i / \hat e(X_i)}{\sum_i T_i / \hat e(X_i)}, \qquad \hat\mu_0^{\text{Hájek}} = \frac{\sum_i (1-T_i) Y_i / (1-\hat e(X_i))}{\sum_i (1-T_i) / (1-\hat e(X_i))}.$$
  Each is a weighted average, so it stays within the range of $Y$. This is the version the lab uses.
- **Trimming**: drop units with $\hat e$ outside, say, $[0.05, 0.95]$. Variance falls, but the estimand changes to "units that could plausibly get either treatment" — say so.
- **ATT weights**: treated units get weight 1; controls get the **odds** $\hat e/(1-\hat e)$, which reweights them to the treated group's case mix. Kidney stones: B-small $0.32$, B-large $3.29$ turn B's 270 small / 80 large into 87 / 263 — exactly A's mix (25 % / 75 %). ATT $= +4.8$ pp.

::: {.notes}
Three standard fixes, each with a cost. Hájek weights normalize within each arm; they trade a tiny bias for much lower variance and can never produce an average outside the range of the outcomes (Horvitz–Thompson can, when weights are large). On the kidney stones both versions give 5.37 pp because the weights already sum to 700 in each arm. Trimming is a legitimate fix but it quietly changes the question: you are now estimating the effect among people who could plausibly have received either treatment. The ATT weights answer "what was the effect for the people who actually got A?". Check the arithmetic aloud: 270 × 0.322 = 87 and 80 × 3.29 = 263, so the reweighted B group has exactly A's 87 small and 263 large patients. ATT weights only require that every kind of A patient has comparable B patients.
:::

## Matching: find each treated unit a twin

**Idea:** for every treated unit, find one or more untreated units with similar covariates and compare outcomes within those pairs. It mimics a randomized experiment *after the fact*. Matching treated units to controls estimates the **ATT**.

- **Distance**: the estimated propensity score $\hat e(X)$, or the *Mahalanobis distance* (covariate distance adjusted for scales and correlations).
- **Design choices**: matches per unit, with or without replacement, and a **caliper** (maximum distance; treated units with no close twin are dropped).
- **Stratification** is a coarse version: cut $\hat e$ into about five strata and compare within each. Cochran (1968): five subclasses remove about 90 % of the bias due to a covariate.

::: {.block .example data-title="Running example: kidney stones"}
Matching each A patient exactly on stone size compares small with small and large with large, then averages over A's case mix (25 % small, 75 % large): ATT $= 0.25 \times 6.4 + 0.75 \times 4.3 \approx$ **+4.8 pp**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Matching is the most intuitive adjustment method: it literally constructs comparable groups. Stress that matching treated to controls targets the ATT — the effect for the kind of patients who received A — which differs from the ATE when effects vary (4.8 versus 5.4 pp here). The arithmetic in the example uses the stratum differences 6.4 and 4.3 pp and A's case mix, 87 small and 263 large out of 350. Calipers improve the quality of matches but drop units, which changes the target population, so report how many were dropped and remember that the estimand is now "treated units that had a comparable control".
:::

## Matching in practice {.deeper .smaller}

- **Check balance — you can!** For each covariate compute the standardized mean difference
  $$\text{SMD} = \frac{\bar x_{T} - \bar x_{C}}{\sqrt{(s_T^2 + s_C^2)/2}}$$
  before and after matching. Rule of thumb: $|\text{SMD}| < 0.1$ afterwards. Unlike ignorability, balance on *observed* covariates is testable.
- **Standard errors need care**: controls are reused and $\hat e$ was estimated. Use Abadie–Imbens standard errors or cluster by matched set; the plain bootstrap is **invalid** for nearest-neighbor matching with replacement (Abadie & Imbens, 2008).
- **Abadie–Imbens bias correction**: with continuous covariates, matches are never exact; a regression on the matched data removes the leftover imbalance.

```r
library(MatchIt); library(marginaleffects)
m  <- matchit(T ~ X1 + X2, data = d, method = "nearest", distance = "glm", caliper = 0.1)
summary(m)                                      # SMDs before and after matching
md <- match.data(m)                             # matched sample with weights and subclass
fit <- lm(Y ~ T * (X1 + X2), data = md, weights = weights)   # regression on matched data
avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "T", vcov = ~subclass,      # SEs clustered by matched pair
                newdata = subset(md, T == 1), wts = "weights")   # average over treated: ATT
```

::: {.notes}
The big practical message: balance diagnostics are one of the few places where the data can tell you that your adjustment failed. If SMDs are still large after matching, change the specification before looking at outcomes. The code follows the MatchIt workflow: nearest-neighbor matching on a logistic-regression propensity score with a caliper of 0.1 standard deviations of the score; summary() prints the balance table; the outcome regression on the matched sample with T × X interactions plays the role of the bias correction, and avg_comparisons with newdata restricted to treated units gives the ATT with standard errors clustered by matched pair.
:::

## Doubly robust estimation (AIPW): the idea {.smaller}

Start with the outcome model's prediction (g-computation). Then check how wrong it was on the units where we **can** see the truth, and add an IPW-weighted average of those errors as a correction:

$$
\hat\tau_{\text{AIPW}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \Big[ \underbrace{\hat\mu_1(X_i) - \hat\mu_0(X_i)}_{\text{g-computation}} + \underbrace{\frac{T_i\,\big(Y_i - \hat\mu_1(X_i)\big)}{\hat e(X_i)} - \frac{(1-T_i)\,\big(Y_i - \hat\mu_0(X_i)\big)}{1 - \hat e(X_i)}}_{\text{IPW-weighted residuals: the correction}} \Big]
$$

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
- If the outcome model is perfect, its residuals average to zero and the correction does nothing.
- If the outcome model is biased, the weighted residuals estimate that bias **for the whole population** (as long as the weights are right) and cancel it.
:::

- AIPW = *augmented* inverse probability weighting (Robins, Rotnitzky & Zhao, 1994). Each bracketed term $\hat\psi_i$ is one unit's contribution, so a standard error is simply $\text{sd}(\hat\psi_i)/\sqrt{n}$.
- Kidney stones: **+5.4 pp** again, with standard error 3.36 pp.

::: {.notes}
Build the formula from its two pieces rather than presenting it whole. The first piece is g-computation from a few slides back. The second piece is IPW applied not to the outcomes but to the outcome model's residuals: for treated units, how far was the actual Y from the predicted mu_1? Weighting those residuals by 1/e makes their average represent the whole population, not just the treated. So the correction estimates the outcome model's average error and subtracts it. A side benefit: because the estimator is an average of per-unit terms psi_i, its standard error is just their standard deviation divided by root n — the code computes it in its last line (technically this is the "influence function" standard error).
:::

## Double robustness: two chances to be right

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 14 (Double robustness)"}
$\hat\tau_{\text{AIPW}}$ is consistent for the ATE if **either** the propensity model $\hat e$ **or** the outcome model $\hat\mu_t$ is correctly specified — it does not need both.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block .intuition data-title="Case 1: propensity model right"}
With the right weights, the correction averages to exactly the outcome model's error, ${\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - \hat\mu_1(X)]}$, and cancels it — however wrong $\hat\mu_1$ was.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block .intuition data-title="Case 2: outcome model right"}
With the right outcome model, the residuals ${Y - \mu_1(X)}$ average to zero at every $X$, whatever the weights: the correction vanishes — however wrong $\hat e$ was.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.block .alert data-title="What double robustness does not do"}
If both models are wrong, there is no guarantee (see the lab). Ignorability and overlap are still required: two chances at modeling, not zero assumptions.
:::

::: {.notes}
The two cases are the whole proof, so it is worth going through them. Case 1 reuses the IPW unbiasedness argument from earlier, applied to the residual Y − mu-hat_1(X) instead of Y. Case 2 uses only that, given X and T = 1, Y has mean mu_1(X), so the residual has conditional mean zero, whatever we divide it by. The same reasoning applies to the control term. A bonus fact for curious students: when both models are right, AIPW reaches the smallest variance achievable without assuming a parametric model (the semiparametric efficiency bound). That does not mean it beats a correctly specified parametric regression — in the lab, linear regression is slightly tighter because its linear model is exactly true.
:::

## In code: IPW and AIPW

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
ps <- fitted(glm(T ~ X1 + X2, family = binomial, data = d))       # ê(X)
tr <- d$T; y <- d$Y
ipw <- mean(tr * y / ps) - mean((1 - tr) * y / (1 - ps))           # Horvitz–Thompson
w1 <- tr / ps; w0 <- (1 - tr) / (1 - ps)
hajek <- sum(w1 * y) / sum(w1) - sum(w0 * y) / sum(w0)             # Hájek (normalized weights)

mu1 <- predict(lm(Y ~ X1 + X2, data = d, subset = T == 1), newdata = d)   # μ̂₁(X)
mu0 <- predict(lm(Y ~ X1 + X2, data = d, subset = T == 0), newdata = d)   # μ̂₀(X)
psi <- mu1 - mu0 + tr * (y - mu1) / ps - (1 - tr) * (y - mu0) / (1 - ps)
c(aipw = mean(psi), se = sd(psi) / sqrt(nrow(d)))                  # SE: sd of the per-unit terms / sqrt(n)
```

### Python

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LinearRegression

e = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf).fit(X, T).predict_proba(X)[:, 1]       # ê(X), C=inf: no penalty
mu1 = LinearRegression().fit(X[T == 1], Y[T == 1]).predict(X)            # μ̂₁(X)
mu0 = LinearRegression().fit(X[T == 0], Y[T == 0]).predict(X)            # μ̂₀(X)

ipw = np.mean(T * Y / e) - np.mean((1 - T) * Y / (1 - e))                # Horvitz–Thompson
w1, w0 = T / e, (1 - T) / (1 - e)
hajek = np.sum(w1 * Y) / np.sum(w1) - np.sum(w0 * Y) / np.sum(w0)        # Hájek
psi = mu1 - mu0 + T * (Y - mu1) / e - (1 - T) * (Y - mu0) / (1 - e)
aipw, se = psi.mean(), psi.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(psi))               # SE: sd of the per-unit terms / sqrt(n)
```
:::

[Here `d` (R) holds columns `Y`, `T` (0/1), `X1`, `X2`; in Python `X` is an $n \times 2$ array and `T`, `Y` are 0/1 and numeric arrays.]{.code-note}

::: {.notes}
Each line maps to a formula from the previous slides: the propensity model, the Horvitz–Thompson and Hájek versions of IPW, the two arm-specific outcome regressions, and the AIPW terms psi. The standard error in the last line is the sd of the per-unit terms over root n, as on the AIPW slide; it treats e-hat and mu-hat as fixed, which is fine asymptotically for AIPW. On the kidney-stone data (with X = a large-stone indicator) this code returns 5.37 pp for all three estimators and a standard error of 3.36 pp.
:::

## Lab: which estimator survives? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{ojs}
viewof labGamma = Inputs.range([0, 2.5], {value: 1.2, step: 0.1, label: "Confounding γ"})
viewof labN = Inputs.range([200, 2000], {value: 500, step: 100, label: "n per replicate"})
viewof labBadE = Inputs.toggle({label: "ê(X) wrong (omits X₂)", value: false})
viewof labBadMu = Inputs.toggle({label: "μ̂(X) wrong (omits X₂)", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
labGammaD = debounce(viewof labGamma)
labND = debounce(viewof labN)
```

::: {.small}
60 simulated datasets, true effect $\tau = 2$:<br>
$T \sim \text{Bernoulli}\big(\text{expit}(\gamma\,(0.7X_1 + 0.9X_2))\big)$<br>
$Y = 1 + 2T + X_1 + 1.5X_2 + \varepsilon$<br>
**Bias** = average estimate − 2 (systematic error) · **SD** = spread across datasets (noise)
:::

```{ojs}
html`<div class="readout" style="font-size:0.92em">${labTable.map(d => `<div>${d.metodo}: bias <b>${d.sesgo.toFixed(2)}</b>, SD ${d.de.toFixed(2)}</div>`).join("")}
<div style="margin-top:6px">${
  labGamma < 0.05 ? "No confounding: treatment is a coin flip, so every method — even the naive difference and the wrong models — is centered on 2."
  : labBadE && labBadMu ? "Both models are wrong: AIPW has nothing left to lean on, so it is biased too. Two chances, not zero assumptions."
  : labBadE ? "The propensity model is wrong, so <b>IPW</b> is biased. <b>AIPW</b> leans on the correct outcome model and stays centered on 2 — double robustness."
  : labBadMu ? (labGamma >= 2 ? "The outcome model is wrong, so <b>regression</b> is biased. <b>AIPW</b> leans on the correct propensity model and stays roughly centered — but with this little overlap its weights are extreme and it gets noisy."
                              : "The outcome model is wrong, so <b>regression</b> is biased. <b>AIPW</b> leans on the correct propensity model and stays centered on 2 — double robustness.")
  : labGamma >= 2 ? "Both models are right, but overlap is poor: <b>IPW</b>'s weights explode, so it is very noisy (and slightly biased). Regression and AIPW cope much better."
  : "Both models are right: every adjusted estimator is centered on 2. Regression is tightest because its linear model is exactly true here; IPW is the noisiest."
}</div></div>`
```
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{ojs}
labRes = {
  const rng = mulberry32(99), n = labND, out = [];
  const dot = (a, b) => { let t = 0; for (let k = 0; k < a.length; k++) t += a[k] * b[k]; return t; };
  for (let r = 0; r < 60; r++) {
    const T = new Float64Array(n), Y = new Float64Array(n), rowsE = [], rows1 = [], rows0 = [], rowsMu = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const x1 = randn(rng), x2 = randn(rng);
      const t = rng() < expit(labGammaD * (0.7 * x1 + 0.9 * x2)) ? 1 : 0;
      T[i] = t; Y[i] = 1 + 2 * t + x1 + 1.5 * x2 + randn(rng);
      // precompute design rows once per replicate
      rowsE.push(labBadE ? [1, x1] : [1, x1, x2]);
      rows1.push(labBadMu ? [1, 1, x1] : [1, 1, x1, x2]);
      rows0.push(labBadMu ? [1, 0, x1] : [1, 0, x1, x2]);
      rowsMu.push(t ? rows1[i] : rows0[i]);
    }
    const bE = logitFit(rowsE, T), bMu = olsFit(rowsMu, Y);
    let m1 = 0, m0 = 0, n1 = 0, sw1 = 0, sw0 = 0, sy1 = 0, sy0 = 0, aipw = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const e = Math.min(0.995, Math.max(0.005, expit(dot(bE, rowsE[i]))));
      const mu1 = dot(bMu, rows1[i]), mu0 = dot(bMu, rows0[i]);
      if (T[i]) { m1 += Y[i]; n1++; sw1 += 1 / e; sy1 += Y[i] / e; }
      else { m0 += Y[i]; sw0 += 1 / (1 - e); sy0 += Y[i] / (1 - e); }
      aipw += mu1 - mu0 + T[i] * (Y[i] - mu1) / e - (1 - T[i]) * (Y[i] - mu0) / (1 - e);
    }
    out.push({metodo: "Naive", est: m1 / n1 - m0 / (n - n1)});
    out.push({metodo: "Regression", est: bMu[1]});
    out.push({metodo: "IPW (Hájek)", est: sy1 / sw1 - sy0 / sw0});
    out.push({metodo: "AIPW", est: aipw / n});
  }
  return out;
}
labTable = d3.groups(labRes, d => d.metodo).map(([metodo, v]) => ({
  metodo, sesgo: d3.mean(v, d => d.est) - 2, de: d3.deviation(v, d => d.est)
}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, marginLeft: 100,
  marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [0.5, 5.5], label: "Effect estimate (60 simulated datasets)", grid: true, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36},
  y: {domain: ["Naive", "Regression", "IPW (Hájek)", "AIPW"], label: null},
  color: {domain: ["Naive", "Regression", "IPW (Hájek)", "AIPW"], range: ["#9aa3b5", "#14213d", "#c8742b", "#2e8b57"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([2], {stroke: "#2e8b57", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6 4"}),
    Plot.boxX(labRes, {x: "est", y: "metodo", fill: "metodo", fillOpacity: 0.35, stroke: "metodo"}),
  ]
})
```

::: {.block .intuition data-title="Three things to try"}
1. Set γ to **0**: with no confounding even the naive difference is right.
2. At γ ≈ 1.2, tick **ê wrong** (IPW breaks, AIPW survives), then **μ̂ wrong** instead (regression breaks, AIPW survives), then **both** (AIPW breaks too).
3. Both models right, push γ to **2.5**: IPW's box balloons — extreme weights, as in the 3D scene.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Give students a minute to play before explaining. Each box summarizes 60 simulated datasets; the dashed line is the truth, 2. The naive difference is badly biased as soon as gamma is positive because treated units have higher X1 and X2, which raise Y. "Wrong" means the model omits X2, a real confounder. The key pattern for double robustness is in experiment 2: each single-model method fails when its own model is wrong, while AIPW fails only when both are. Experiment 3 connects to positivity: with strong confounding some propensities are near 0 or 1, IPW weights blow up, and the estimate becomes noisy (it is also slightly biased here because the weights are clipped at 0.005 and 0.995). Note that with both models right, regression is tighter than AIPW: the linear model is exactly true in this simulation, and a correct parametric model is hard to beat.
:::

## Double/debiased machine learning {.deeper .smaller}

**The problem.** With many covariates, linear models for $\mu_t$ and $e$ are probably wrong. Machine learning (random forests, boosting, lasso) can learn these *nuisance functions* — needed, but not what we care about — flexibly.

**The trap.** Plug ML predictions into regression or IPW and $\hat\tau$ inherits ML's regularization bias (ML deliberately trades bias for variance). The bias shrinks too slowly, and confidence intervals are wrong.

**Two fixes** (Chernozhukov et al., 2018):

- **Orthogonality** — use the AIPW score. Errors in $\hat\mu$ and $\hat e$ enter $\hat\tau$ only through their **product**, roughly $\|\hat\mu - \mu\| \times \|\hat e - e\|$, so two moderately accurate models give a very accurate $\hat\tau$. Requirement: the product shrinks faster than $1/\sqrt{n}$ (e.g. each error faster than $n^{-1/4}$).
- **Cross-fitting** — split the data into $K$ folds; fit the nuisance models on $K-1$ folds and compute the score on the held-out fold; rotate. No unit is scored by a model that was trained on it.

**Result:** $\hat\tau$ is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and approximately normal, so ordinary confidence intervals work. Relatives: **TMLE** (van der Laan & Rubin, 2006) targets the outcome model with a small update step; **causal forests** (Wager & Athey, 2018) estimate $\text{CATE}(x)$ with confidence intervals.

::: {.notes}
Optional slide. The one-sentence version: AIPW plus cross-fitting lets you use any good machine-learning model for the nuisance functions and still get valid confidence intervals for the effect. Why the product of errors? The AIPW estimator's bias, to first order, is the average of (e − e-hat) × (mu − mu-hat) / e-hat; if each error is of order n to the minus 1/4, the product is of order n to the minus 1/2 and is swamped by sampling noise. That is what "Neyman orthogonality" buys. For the curious: the AIPW term psi is the efficient influence function of the ATE, and its variance is the semiparametric efficiency bound (Hahn, 1998). Cross-fitting avoids the overfitting bias that would arise if a flexible model scored the very units it memorized.
:::

## In code: double ML and causal forests {.deeper}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R · DoubleML

```r
library(DoubleML); library(mlr3); library(mlr3learners)
dml_data <- double_ml_data_from_data_frame(d, y_col = "Y", d_cols = "T", x_cols = c("X1", "X2"))
irm <- DoubleMLIRM$new(dml_data,
                       ml_g = lrn("regr.ranger", min.node.size = 20),     # outcome model μ̂_t(x)
                       ml_m = lrn("classif.ranger", min.node.size = 20),  # propensity model ê(x)
                       n_folds = 5)                    # 5-fold cross-fitting
irm$fit(); irm$summary()                               # ATE with standard error and CI
```

### R · grf

```r
library(grf)
cf <- causal_forest(X = as.matrix(d[, c("X1", "X2")]), Y = d$Y, W = d$T)
average_treatment_effect(cf, target.sample = "all")   # ATE via AIPW with forest nuisances
tau_x <- predict(cf)$predictions                      # CATE(x_i), out-of-bag
```

### Python · DoubleML

```python
import doubleml as dml
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, RandomForestClassifier

data = dml.DoubleMLData(df, y_col="Y", d_cols="T", x_cols=["X1", "X2"])
irm = dml.DoubleMLIRM(data, ml_g=RandomForestRegressor(min_samples_leaf=20),
                      ml_m=RandomForestClassifier(min_samples_leaf=20), n_folds=5)   # big leaves: no ê of exactly 0 or 1
irm.fit()
print(irm.summary)      # ATE, standard error, 95% CI
```
:::

::: {.notes}
DoubleMLIRM is the "interactive regression model": binary treatment, fully flexible outcome and propensity functions, AIPW score with cross-fitting — exactly the previous slide. ml_g is the outcome learner and ml_m the propensity learner. The minimum leaf size of 20 matters: a default random-forest classifier can output propensities of exactly 0 or 1, which produces infinite weights in the AIPW score — DoubleML then warns and the standard errors come out several times too large. Larger leaves keep e-hat away from 0 and 1, the overlap lesson again. grf's causal forest fits the nuisance functions with forests and then reports an AIPW-type ATE; its main strength is estimating how the effect varies with covariates, CATE(x). With only two covariates and a linear truth these tools are overkill; they pay off with dozens of covariates and nonlinear relationships.
:::

## Classical inference: how sure are we?

- **Standard error (SE)**: how much $\hat\tau$ would vary if we drew a new sample. Kidney stones: SE = 3.36 pp.
- **95 % confidence interval** $= \hat\tau \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$, from large-sample normality. Kidney stones: ${5.37 \pm 1.96 \times 3.36} \approx$ **[−1.2, +11.9] pp** — compatible with no effect.
- **Getting the SE right**: sandwich (Huber–White) SEs for regression; for AIPW, $\text{sd}(\hat\psi_i)/\sqrt{n}$ from its per-unit terms; for IPW and AIPW, a bootstrap that refits $\hat e$ in every resample (but not for nearest-neighbor matching with replacement); randomization inference for small experiments.

::: {.block .alert data-title="The most misunderstood sentence in statistics"}
A 95 % CI comes with a guarantee about the **procedure**: across repeated samples, 95 % of such intervals cover $\tau$. It does **not** say $\mathbb{P}(\tau \in [-1.2, 11.9] \mid \text{data}) = 0.95$. That is a Bayesian statement — coming up.
:::

::: {.notes}
Students know confidence intervals, but the causal setting adds two lessons. First, the uncertainty must account for every estimated piece, including the propensity model — that is why the bootstrap must refit e-hat inside each resample. Sandwich standard errors stay valid when the error variance differs across units or the regression is only an approximation; the plain bootstrap fails for nearest-neighbor matching with replacement (Abadie and Imbens, 2008). Second, the kidney-stone answer is a good reality check: adjustment fixed the bias (the sign flipped from −4.6 to +5.4 pp), but with 700 patients the interval still includes zero. Adjustment fixes bias, not noise. The alert box sets up the Bayesian section: if you want the probability that A is better given these data, you need a prior and a posterior.
:::

## What does "95% confidence" mean? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{ojs}
viewof ciDraw = Inputs.button("Draw 50 new samples")
viewof ciLevel = Inputs.radio([0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99], {value: 0.95, label: "Level", format: d => `${100 * d}%`})
```

```{ojs}
ciRows = {
  const rng = mulberry32(1000 + ciDraw), n = 25, z = qnorm(1 - (1 - ciLevel) / 2), rows = [];
  for (let k = 0; k < 50; k++) {
    let s = 0; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) s += 2 + randn(rng);
    const m = s / n, h = z / Math.sqrt(n);
    rows.push({k, lo: m - h, hi: m + h, m, cubre: m - h <= 2 && 2 <= m + h});
  }
  return rows;
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 380, marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [1, 3], label: "τ", grid: true, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36}, y: {axis: null},
  color: {domain: [true, false], range: ["#14213d", "#d1495b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([2], {stroke: "#2e8b57", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.link(ciRows, {x1: "lo", x2: "hi", y1: "k", y2: "k", stroke: "cubre", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(ciRows, {x: "m", y: "k", r: 2.5, fill: "cubre"})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
```{ojs}
html`<div class="readout">Intervals covering τ = 2: <b>${ciRows.filter(d => d.cubre).length} of 50</b><br>(nominal: ${100 * ciLevel}%)</div>`
```

Each line is the confidence interval from a **new sample** of 25 observations; the green line is the true $\tau = 2$. Intervals that miss are red.

- Press the button a few times: at 95 % about 47–48 of 50 cover on average — sometimes 45, sometimes 50.
- Switch to 80 %: intervals get shorter and about 10 in 50 miss.

The probability belongs to the **procedure**. Any single interval either covers $\tau$ or it does not.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Let students predict before pressing: "If I draw 50 samples, how many intervals will miss?" Then press several times. The count fluctuates around 47.5 at the 95 percent level. The point to land: once you have computed one interval from your data, it either contains tau or it does not — there is no 95 percent left in it. The 95 percent describes how often the method works across hypothetical repetitions. The question "how probable is tau > 0 given these data?" requires a Bayesian answer, which is where the deck goes next.
:::

## Recap: Classical estimation {.recap}

- Identification gives a formula; estimation needs a model of the **outcome** (regression, g-computation), of the **treatment** (IPW, matching), or **both** (AIPW).
- A regression coefficient is the ATE only if the model is right and the effect is homogeneous; g-computation predicts both potential outcomes for everyone and averages.
- The propensity score compresses many covariates into one number; IPW turns each group into a pseudo-population that looks like everyone. Huge weights signal poor overlap.
- AIPW combines both models and survives if either one is right; with machine learning and cross-fitting it becomes double/debiased ML.
- Kidney stones: standardization, IPW and AIPW give **+5.4 pp** (regression 5.38); matching targets the ATT (**+4.8 pp**); 95 % CI ≈ **[−1.2, 11.9]** — a property of the procedure, not of this interval.

[**Test yourself:** why does IPW give each small-stone patient who got A a weight of about 4?]{.small}

::: {.notes}
If students remember one thing from this section: the estimators differ in which model they trust — the outcome model, the treatment model, or either — and none of them can repair a failure of identification. Everything here assumed all confounders were measured. The next section asks what to do when they are not. Answer to the test-yourself question: only 87 of 357 small-stone patients (24 percent) got A, so each of them stands in for 1/0.244 ≈ 4.1 small-stone patients — the ones who got B included — and the reweighted A group then has the population's 357 small-stone patients.
:::

# When Confounders Are Unobserved {#designs .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Natural experiments and sensitivity analysis.]{.section-subtitle}

```{=html}
<div class="pipeline"><div><b>1 · Question</b></div><div><b>2 · Estimand</b></div><div class="on"><b>3 · Identification</b></div><div class="on"><b>4 · Estimation</b></div><div class="on"><b>5 · Uncertainty</b></div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
Everything in the last section assumed we had measured every confounder. This section is about what to do when we know we haven't. There are two answers: find a natural experiment that sidesteps the unmeasured confounder, or ask how strong that confounder would have to be to change our conclusion. Stages 3 to 5 of the pipeline are all in play.
:::

## Four natural experiments {.smaller}

Adjustment needs **every** confounder measured. If some $U$ is missing, no regression or weighting can fix it. Instead, look for a **natural experiment**: some feature of the world that makes treatment *as good as random* for one particular comparison.

| Design | Compare… | Works if… | Estimates | Classic example |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Difference in differences** | the *change* from before to after, treated vs. untreated group | both groups would have changed equally without treatment | effect on the treated (ATT) | minimum wage: New Jersey vs. Pennsylvania (Card & Krueger 1994) |
| **Instrumental variables** | people nudged toward treatment vs. not nudged | the nudge is random and affects $Y$ only through $T$ | effect for the people the nudge moves (*compliers*, defined below) | the Vietnam draft lottery (Angrist 1990) |
| **Regression discontinuity** | just above vs. just below a cutoff | nothing except treatment jumps at the cutoff | effect *at* the cutoff | merit awards above a test score (Thistlethwaite & Campbell 1960) |
| **Synthetic control** | one treated unit vs. a weighted blend of untreated units | the blend that tracked it before would have kept tracking | effect on that unit, over time | California's 1988 tobacco program (Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller 2010) |

::: {.block .example data-title="Could a design rescue the kidney stones?"}
Suppose which surgeon happened to be on call partly decided A vs. B. The on-call rota is unrelated to stone size or frailty, so it would be an **instrument**: it is the "Z · doctor on call" from the adjust-or-not quiz in Section 3.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the map of the section. The point to land: we are not getting rid of assumptions, we are swapping one assumption (all confounders measured) for another one that may be more believable in a given setting. Walk through one row as an example, say Card and Krueger: Pennsylvania's change in fast-food employment stands in for what would have happened in New Jersey without the minimum-wage increase. The kidney-stone bridge matters: in Section 3 the doctor on call was a variable you did not need to adjust for; here the same kind of variable becomes useful in a completely different way. Each of the next slides takes one row and unpacks it.
:::

## Difference in differences: the idea {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{ojs}
viewof dzDrift = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "Extra trend in the treated group"})
```

```{ojs}
dzDid = {
  const ctrl0 = 10, ctrl1 = 13, tr0 = 14, effect = 5;
  const assumed = tr0 + (ctrl1 - ctrl0);   // counterfactual if trends are parallel
  const trNo1 = assumed + dzDrift;         // true counterfactual: treated, after, no treatment
  const tr1 = trNo1 + effect;              // observed: treated, after
  return {ctrl0, ctrl1, tr0, tr1, trNo1, assumed, effect, did: (tr1 - tr0) - (ctrl1 - ctrl0)};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 340, marginRight: 150, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], ticks: [0, 1], tickFormat: d => d === 0 ? "Before" : "After", label: null},
  y: {domain: [8, 26], label: "Average outcome", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([[0, dzDid.ctrl0], [1, dzDid.ctrl1]], {stroke: "#14213d", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line([[0, dzDid.tr0], [1, dzDid.tr1]], {stroke: "#c8742b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line([[0, dzDid.tr0], [1, dzDid.assumed]], {stroke: "#c8742b", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "7 5"}),
    dzDrift !== 0 ? Plot.line([[0, dzDid.tr0], [1, dzDid.trNo1]], {stroke: "#6b7385", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "2 4"}) : null,
    Plot.dot([[0, dzDid.ctrl0], [1, dzDid.ctrl1]], {r: 5, fill: "#14213d"}),
    Plot.dot([[0, dzDid.tr0], [1, dzDid.tr1]], {r: 5, fill: "#c8742b"}),
    Plot.text([
      {x: 1, y: dzDid.tr1, t: "Treated (observed)"},
      {x: 1, y: dzDid.ctrl1, t: "Control (observed)"},
      {x: 1, y: dzDid.assumed, t: "Assumed counterfactual"},
      ...(dzDrift !== 0 ? [{x: 1, y: dzDid.trNo1, t: "True counterfactual"}] : [])
    ], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", dx: 10, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 13})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
```{ojs}
html`<div class="readout">
  DiD estimate: <b>${dzDid.did.toFixed(2)}</b> &nbsp;(true effect: 5)<br>
  Bias: <b>${(dzDid.did - dzDid.effect).toFixed(2)}</b><br>
  <span style="color:#5b6478">After-only comparison: ${(dzDid.tr1 - dzDid.ctrl1).toFixed(2)} · Before–after in treated: ${(dzDid.tr1 - dzDid.tr0).toFixed(2)}</span><br><br>
  ${dzDrift === 0 ? "Parallel trends hold: the control group's change (+3) is exactly what the treated group would have done, so DiD recovers 5."
                  : "Parallel trends fail: the treated group was drifting on its own, and DiD wrongly credits that drift to the treatment."}
</div>`
```

The treated group starts **higher** and both groups **rise over time**, so neither simple comparison works. DiD uses the control group's change (+3) as a stand-in for how the treated group would have changed without treatment.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Start with the slider at zero. Ask: why not just compare the two groups after the policy? Because they differed before it (14 vs 10), so you get 9, not 5. Why not compare the treated group before and after? Because everything rose by 3 anyway, so you get 8. DiD subtracts both: (22 − 14) − (13 − 10) = 5. Then move the slider: if the treated group was on its own steeper path, DiD absorbs that drift into the estimate one for one. The bias equals exactly the violation of parallel trends — that is the whole assumption in one picture.
:::

## Difference in differences: the formal statement {.smaller}

Two periods, *pre* and *post*. $T = 1$ marks the group treated in the post period; $Y^{\text{post}}(0)$ is its post-period outcome *without* treatment.

$$
\tau_{\text{DiD}} = \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}[Y^{\text{post}} \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y^{\text{pre}} \mid T=1]\big)}_{\text{change in the treated group}} - \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}[Y^{\text{post}} \mid T=0] - \mathbb{E}[Y^{\text{pre}} \mid T=0]\big)}_{\text{change in the control group}}
$$

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 15 (Identification by DiD)"}
Assume **parallel trends**, $\;\mathbb{E}[Y^{\text{post}}(0) - Y^{\text{pre}}(0) \mid T=1] = \mathbb{E}[Y^{\text{post}}(0) - Y^{\text{pre}}(0) \mid T=0]$, and **no anticipation** (treatment does not change outcomes before it starts). Then $\tau_{\text{DiD}} = \text{ATT}$, the effect on the treated group in the post period.
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
The treated group's change = its own untreated trend + the effect. Parallel trends says its untreated trend equals the control group's change, so subtracting that change leaves only the effect. The groups may differ in **level**; they must not differ in **trend**.
:::

::: {.notes}
We write pre and post as superscripts so they don't collide with the potential-outcome labels Y(1) and Y(0). Point out what the assumption does NOT require: the groups can be very different in their levels — New Jersey and Pennsylvania need not have the same employment. They only need to move together absent the policy. That is weaker than ignorability in one way (level differences are fine) and stronger in another (it is about trends, which we can only partly check). It is a statement about the untreated potential outcome, which we never observe for the treated group after treatment, so it cannot be tested directly.
:::

## Difference in differences in practice {.smaller}

- **Check pre-trends.** With several periods before treatment, plot the treated–control gap period by period (an *event study*). If the gap was already drifting before the policy, parallel trends is in doubt. This is the most convincing diagnostic DiD has — but it can't prove the trends would have *stayed* parallel.
- **Estimate with a regression.** With one treated group, one control group and two periods, regress $Y$ on a treated-group indicator, a post-period indicator and their product. The coefficient on the product *is* the DiD.

::: {.block .alert data-title="Back to the cameras"}
Cameras usually go where crashes just spiked. Part of that spike would have faded anyway (regression to the mean), so camera sites would *not* have trended like other sites: parallel trends fails, and DiD overstates the effect.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
# one row per unit and period; treated = 1 for the treated group, post = 1 after the policy
fit <- lm(y ~ treated * post, data = df)              # coefficient on treated:post = the 2x2 DiD
lmtest::coeftest(fit, vcov = sandwich::vcovCL, cluster = ~ id)   # standard errors clustered by unit
```

### Python

```python
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
fit = smf.ols("y ~ treated * post", data=df).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["id"]})
print(fit.params["treated:post"])   # the 2x2 DiD estimate
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The camera example from the opening slide is the classic failure mode: units are selected into treatment because of a temporary shock, and the shock reverses on its own. Labor economists call the same thing Ashenfelter's dip: people join job-training programs right after their earnings fall, and earnings would have recovered anyway. In the code, the coefficient on the interaction treated:post is exactly the 2×2 DiD from the previous slide; clustering by unit accounts for repeated observations of the same unit.
:::

## Staggered adoption {.deeper}

Often units start treatment at **different times** (states adopt a policy in different years).

- The traditional tool is the **two-way fixed-effects** (TWFE) regression: regress $Y$ on a dummy for each unit, a dummy for each period, and an indicator for "treated now".
- With staggered timing, TWFE quietly uses **already-treated** units as controls for later adopters. If effects grow or shrink over time, the estimate can be badly biased — even the wrong sign (Goodman-Bacon 2021; de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfœuille 2020).
- Modern estimators (Callaway & Sant'Anna 2021; Sun & Abraham 2021) compare each adoption cohort only with **not-yet-treated or never-treated** units, then average.

```r
library(did)   # Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021); first_treat = period first treated, 0 if never
out <- att_gt(yname = "y", tname = "year", idname = "id", gname = "first_treat",
              data = panel, control_group = "notyettreated")
ggdid(aggte(out, type = "dynamic"))   # event study: pre-treatment estimates should hover near 0
```

::: {.notes}
Why does TWFE go wrong? A unit treated in 2015 serves as a "control" for a unit treated in 2018 — but by 2018 the first unit's outcome already contains its own (possibly growing) treatment effect, so subtracting its change removes part of the effect we are trying to measure. The fix is conceptually simple: only compare against units that are not yet treated. The did package does this and then aggregates the cohort-specific effects into an event-study plot.
:::

## Instrumental variables: the idea

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 -10 600 250" width="100%" style="font-family:'Source Sans 3',sans-serif">
  <defs>
    <marker id="dzAh" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#14213d"/></marker>
    <marker id="dzAhRed" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#d1495b"/></marker>
  </defs>

    <circle cx="70" cy="150" r="26"/><circle cx="260" cy="150" r="26"/><circle cx="530" cy="150" r="26"/>
    <line x1="96" y1="150" x2="230" y2="150" marker-end="url(#dzAh)"/>
    <line x1="286" y1="150" x2="500" y2="150" marker-end="url(#dzAh)"/>
    <line x1="380" y1="62" x2="282" y2="134" stroke-dasharray="6 5" marker-end="url(#dzAh)"/>
    <line x1="420" y1="62" x2="510" y2="132" stroke-dasharray="6 5" marker-end="url(#dzAh)"/>

  </g>
  <g fill="#14213d" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="central" font-style="italic" font-size="26">
    <text x="400" y="45">U</text><text x="70" y="150">Z</text><text x="260" y="150">T</text><text x="530" y="150">Y</text>
  </g>
  <g fill="#5b6478" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17">
    <text x="400" y="4">unmeasured (e.g. ambition)</text>
    <text x="70" y="196">drafted</text><text x="260" y="196">served</text><text x="530" y="196">earnings</text>
  </g>
  <g fill="#d1495b" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17" font-weight="600">

  </g>
</svg>
```

::: {.block .example data-title="Example: the Vietnam-era draft lottery (Angrist 1990)"}
A lottery on birth dates decided who could be **drafted**; being drafted is the instrument $Z$. Comparing drafted vs. non-drafted men — not veterans vs. non-veterans — avoids "who volunteers?" confounding.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
**Problem:** an unmeasured $U$ drives both $T$ and $Y$, so comparing treated with untreated is biased.

**Idea:** find a **nudge** $Z$ that changes $T$ for reasons unrelated to $U$, and that reaches $Y$ **only through** $T$. Such a $Z$ is called an **instrument**.

The variation in $T$ caused by $Z$ is then "clean": a randomized experiment hidden inside an observational study.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Make the logic concrete: veterans and non-veterans differ in many unmeasured ways, so comparing their earnings is confounded. But the lottery was literally random, so drafted and non-drafted men are comparable on everything, including U. If being drafted affects earnings at all, it must be because it changed who served. The red dashed arrow is the crucial thing that must be absent. A student might ask whether that's true here: some men stayed in college to avoid the draft, which would be a path from Z to Y not through T. That's exactly the kind of argument IV papers have to fight about.
:::

## Instrumental variables: the four conditions

::: {.compact}
| Condition | In symbols | In words | Checkable? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Relevance** | $\operatorname{Cov}(Z, T) \neq 0$ | the nudge actually moves treatment | ✓ yes: look at the data |
| **Independence** | $Z \perp\!\!\!\perp \big(Y(t), T(z)\big)$ | the nudge is as good as random | partly: balance on observed $X$ |
| **Exclusion** | $Y(t, z) = Y(t)$ | the nudge affects $Y$ only through $T$ | ✗ no: argued from subject knowledge |
| **Monotonicity** | $T(1) \geq T(0)$ for everyone | nobody is pushed *away* from treatment by the nudge | ✗ no: argued from subject knowledge |
:::

Here $T(z)$ is a **potential treatment**: the treatment a unit would take if the instrument were set to $z$. Just as each unit has two potential outcomes, it has two potential treatments.

::: {.block .alert data-title="The hard part"}
Relevance is easy to check. **Exclusion** is where IV analyses succeed or fail: it is a claim about a missing arrow, and no data can confirm it.
:::

::: {.notes}
The new idea here is potential treatments: T(1) is whether you would serve if drafted, T(0) whether you would serve if not drafted. Monotonicity says nobody does the opposite of what the nudge suggests. Go down the "checkable?" column: this is honest bookkeeping about which assumptions the data can support and which rest on argument. A good IV paper spends most of its pages defending exclusion.
:::

## Who does IV tell us about? Compliers {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Sort people by how their treatment responds to being drafted ($Z{=}1$):

| Type | $T$ if $Z{=}0$ | $T$ if $Z{=}1$ | In words |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:--|
| **Complier** | 0 | 1 | serves only if drafted |
| Always-taker | 1 | 1 | volunteers anyway |
| Never-taker | 0 | 0 | exempt either way |
| Defier | 1 | 0 | ruled out by monotonicity |

Always- and never-takers ignore $Z$, so by exclusion $Z$ cannot change their $Y$ either. **All** of $Z$'s effect on $Y$ flows through the compliers.

Under monotonicity the denominator below is exactly the **share of compliers**: $\mathbb{E}[T \mid Z{=}1] - \mathbb{E}[T \mid Z{=}0] = \mathbb{P}(\text{complier})$, because always-takers serve either way and there are no defiers.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 16 (LATE; Imbens & Angrist, 1994)"}
Under the four conditions,
$$\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=0]}{\mathbb{E}[T \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[T \mid Z=0]} = \mathbb{E}\big[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid \text{complier}\big].$$
:::

::: {.block .intuition data-title="In plain words"}
**Numerator:** the effect of being *drafted* on earnings. **Denominator:** the share of men the draft moved into service (the compliers). Dividing rescales "effect per drafted man" into "effect per man who served because of the draft". *Illustration:* if being drafted lowers average earnings by \$400 and raises the chance of serving by 0.20, the effect for compliers is −\$400&nbsp;/&nbsp;0.20&nbsp;=&nbsp;−\$2,000.
:::
:::
